articles.title: Central Asia's Hijab Debate Flares Up As Schools Reopen
articles.summary: The hijab has long been a hot topic in Muslim-majority Central Asia, where many authoritarian governments have suppressed Islamic political and religious groups and any outward signs of religiosity. The debate has been rekindled as the new academic year started this month.

articles.title: In US-China AI Race, Kazakhstan Faces Pressure To Pick A Side
articles.summary: Kazakhstan is the only country to have joined both a US-led artificial intelligence initiative and a China-led rival. Now Washington is signaling that it may not be possible to sit on both sides of the emerging AI divide.

articles.summary: Two hundred years after the publication of a book by Jacques Francois Gamba that captured life in the Caucasus in the early 1800s, the work has been published in the Georgian language for the first time.

articles.title: Men Arrested Near UK Air Base Used By US Forces In Iran War
articles.summary: As the conflict in the Persian Gulf continues to impact and shape the region, journalists from RFE/RL's Central Newsroom and Iranian service, Radio Farda, deliver ongoing updates and analysis.

articles.title: Russian Strikes On Ukraine As Zelenskyy Says Russia Not Ready To End War
articles.summary: Russian drone strikes killed at least four people in Ukraine overnight and into September 27.

articles.title: Attack On Security Checkpoint In Pakistan Kills 13, Injures Dozens More
articles.summary: Thirteen people were killed and at least 35 others injured following a blast at a security checkpoint in Dera Ismail Khan, near the border between Pakistan's Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provinces.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Calls On Trump To Enact Russia Sanctions After Deadly Attacks Across Ukraine
articles.summary: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on US President Donald Trump to enact sanctions against Russia amid its deadly attacks across Ukraine, which have become increasingly frequent as cold weather starts to set in.

articles.title: Ukrainian Soldiers Brave Russian Drones On Trek To Frontline Settlements
articles.summary: Ukrainian troops trek nearly 20 kilometers to reach Bilozerske in the embattled Donetsk region. Russian drone and aerial attacks have laid waste to the city that used to house 15,000 inhabitants. Speaking with RFE/RL, one soldier said that "everything is bad" near Dobropillia.

articles.title: As Deadline Looms, Ex-US Marine Desperately Seeks Brother At Afghan Refugee Camp In Qatar
articles.summary: A former US Marine has spent days trying to see his brother at a camp in Qatar holding Afghan refugees in limbo after plans to bring them to the United States were blocked by a presidential executive order. The camp is due to close on September 30, and the inmates don’t know what will happen next.

articles.title: Deadly New Strikes In Russia's War On Ukraine As Spillover Concerns Mount
articles.summary: Russia kept up its pattern of relentless attacks on Kyiv, killing a 14-year-old boy and injuring seven other people in a drone strike on an apartment building in the capital on September 25, Ukrainian authorities said.

articles.title: As Trump Courts Xi, Pressure Mounts To Confront China Over Support For Iran
articles.summary: US lawmakers and national-security experts are pressing President Donald Trump to take tougher action against Chinese entities accused of helping Iran with satellite intelligence, weapons components, and oil revenue.

articles.title: Geran-4 Unpacked: What Makes Russia's New Jet-Powered Drone So Dangerous?
articles.summary: RFE/RL takes apart a Russian Geran-4 drone to uncover what makes the jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) faster, harder to intercept, and capable of operating deep inside Ukraine -- from its turbojet engine and advanced camera to foreign-made communications and navigation components.

articles.title: US Pushes To Turn Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Deal Into Investment Opportunity
articles.summary: The Trump administration is trying to turn a US-brokered opening between Armenia and Azerbaijan into something more tangible: a transport corridor linking Central Asia and the South Caucasus with Western markets -- and an investment opportunity for American companies.

articles.title: US Company That Sold Phone Hacking Software To Pentagon, Secret Service Lied About Russian Ownership, Officials Say
articles.summary: A US company that provided digital forensics and data-extraction software to the Pentagon and other government agencies was in fact owned by a Russian company that also sold software to Russian spy agencies, US authorities charged.

articles.title: US Invites Putin To G20 Summit In Miami, Rubio Says
articles.summary: The United States has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on September 23, as the Trump administration is seeking steps to reduce fighting in Ukraine.

articles.title: Amid Russian Provocations And Warnings Over Possible Attack, Europe Mulls Contingency Plans
articles.summary: In the wake of intelligence reports that Russia may be planning an attack on NATO, questions have arisen over whether European officials have contingency plans ready to deal with such an event.

articles.title: An Afghan Mother And Her Daughters Left Their Homeland In Search Of A Better Life. They Died Of Thirst
articles.summary: At least 17 Afghans died of extreme dehydration in mid-September after crossing Iran through Pakistan, according to a human rights organization. Among them were a mother and her four daughters.

articles.title: US Set To Unveil Next Steps for Trump-Backed Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Corridor
articles.summary: The United States is set to unveil the next stage of TRIPP, a planned transport corridor through southern Armenia that Washington says could open new trade routes linking the South Caucasus and Central Asia with Western markets.

articles.title: Iranian Hard-Liners Up In Arms After Araqchi-Witkoff Meeting In New York
articles.summary: US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi met in New York on September 22 following days of signals that US-Iranian talks would take place on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The meeting sparked a backlash from Iranian hard-liners.

articles.title: Investigation: Amid Setbacks In The Sahel, Russia Quietly Builds Ties In Madagascar
articles.summary: Russia’s efforts to cultivate clout in Africa’s Sahel have been a mixed bag of successes and setbacks. Across the continent, however, on the Indian Ocean island of Madagascar, Moscow is making another quiet push for influence.

articles.title: Can Belarus Replace Canada As US Potash Provider?
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has said a “massive deal” is being discussed with Belarus, under which it would provide cheaper potash supplies than Canada. But questions since the announcement have swirled over whether Belarus can replace the world's largest potash producer to meet US needs.

https://hrf.org/latest/china-marks-12-ye.body: @HRF View post Today marks 12 years since the Chinese regime sentenced Ilham Tohti, a respected Uyghur economist and academic, to life in prison for “separatism.” Ilham peacefully advocated for Uyghur rights through data, research, education, and open dialogue. Before his arrest in January 2014, Ilham taught economics at Minzu University in Beijing and ran a website discussing social and economic issues affecting Uyghurs. He advocated for policies to address poverty, unemployment, and ethnic tensions and promoted greater understanding between Uyghurs and Han Chinese. After a two-day, closed-door trial in September 2014, a Chinese court convicted Ilham of “separatism” and sentenced him to life in prison. His appeal was rejected in a hearing held inside the detention center and without his lawyer present. @JewherIlham has reportedly been held in solitary confinement, and his family has been denied visits since 2017. UN experts have raised concerns about his health and access to medical care. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found his detention arbitrary and linked it to violations of his rights to freedom of expression and due process. Ilham’s continued imprisonment reflects Beijing’s broader repression of Uyghur intellectuals, writers, and academics. HRF condemns the Chinese regime’s continued imprisonment of Ilham, demands his immediate and unconditional release, and calls for his unrestricted access to his family and independent counsel. https://rsf.org/fr/la-libert%C3%A9-dexpr.body: “La liberté d'expression contre la liberté de la presse ?” : lancement d’un livre plaidoyer pour le journalisme au profit de RSF Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Ce 25 septembre 2026, Thibaut Bruttin, directeur de Reporters sans frontières (RSF), publie, dans la collection Libelle des éditions du Seuil, l’essai La liberté d’expression contre la liberté de la presse , plaidoyer pour le journalisme face au culte du free speech , dont 100 % des droits d’auteur seront reversés à l’ONG RSF. Dans l’essai La Liberté d'expression contre la liberté de la presse ? , Thibaut Bruttin, à la tête de RSF depuis juillet 2024, alerte sur le risque de disparition du journalisme comme force centrale dans le débat public et met en évidence une lame de fond géopolitique : le dévoiement et l ’instrumentalisation de la liberté d’expression par l’administration du président américain Donald Trump , invoquée à tout bout de champ, pour promouvoir ses intérêts. L’ouvrage revient, en une centaine de pages, sur les fondements juridiques et les définitions de la liberté de la presse et de la liberté d’expression, mettant en évidence la réécriture américaine de l’histoire constitutionnelle et politique du premier amendement, principal texte à opérer la distinction entre les deux notions. Il montre également l’usage fort peu diplomatique du free speech de l’administration Trump, employé comme prétexte pour déréguler les plateformes technologiques et faire pression aussi bien sur le Brésil que sur l’Union européenne. Pire encore : la méthode Trump fonctionne et fait des émules à travers le monde, tentés d’avoir recours à la violence verbale contre la presse et à la délégitimation répétée des journalistes, aux “faits alternatifs” et aux fariboles érigées en récit politique, encourageant la polarisation à outrance, et de parler aux influenceurs au détriment des professionnels des médias. Dénonçant une offensive mondiale contre l’intégrité de l’information par un dévoiement du free speech ,Thibaut Bruttin appelle à un New Deal pour le journalisme , au respect d’un vrai pluralisme et à la mobilisation autour du droit à l’information, vecteur d’engagement citoyen. Les États-Unis pourraient-ils aspirer à un modèle de société inédit où les faits ne sont plus qu’une opinion parmi d’autres ? Liberté d’expression ou liberté de la presse ? Les deux, répond ce livre ! L’ouvrage est dédié à Christophe Deloire, directeur général de RSF de 2012 à 2024, que le Journal du dimanche , sur sa une du 18 février 2024, osa désigner comme un fossoyeur de la liberté d’expression. 100 % des droits d’auteur seront reversés à RSF. Thibaut Bruttin est directeur général de RSF. Depuis 2014, il contribue au développement d’initiatives clés comme la Journalism Trust Initiative, les évacuations de journalistes afghans et les centres de la liberté de la presse en Ukraine. Par ailleurs historien du cinéma, il a publié plusieurs ouvrages, dont le plus récent est Michel Audiard-Jean Herman/Vautrin (Actes Sud/Institut Lumière, 2023). Publié le 24.09.2026 Europe - Asie centrale France Amériques États-Unis Indépendance et pluralisme Actualité Liberté de la presse

https://rsf.org/fr/le-silence-n-est-plus.body: “Le silence n’est plus une option” : plus de 130 journalistes du monde entier se mobilisent pour Dawit Isaak et ses confrères, enfermés arbitrairement en Érythrée depuis 25 ans Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Vingt-cinq ans après leur arrestation, Dawit Isaak, Temesgen Ghebreyesus, Seyoum Tsehaye et Amanuel Asrat restent détenus au secret, sans jugement, et sans accès à leurs proches. À l’occasion de ce quart de siècle de détention arbitraire, Reporters sans frontières (RSF) et 133 journalistes emblématiques du monde entier appellent la communauté internationale à tout mettre en œuvre pour obtenir leur libération. Lire l'appel mondial ici L’appel mondial de 133 journalistes pour la libération de Dawit Isaak et ses trois confrères Ils sont les journalistes détenus sans procès depuis le plus longtemps au monde. Le 23 septembre 2026 marque les 25 ans de la détention du journaliste suédo-érythréen Dawit Isaak et de ses confrères érythréens Temesgen Ghebreyesus , Seyoum Tsehaye et Amanuel Asrat . Ils ont été arrêtés en septembre 2001 dans la capitale, Asmara, lors d’une vague de répression des autorités érythréennes contre les voix critiques, dont celles de la presse indépendante. Cofondateur et copropriétaire du journal indépendant Setit , Dawit Isaak avait notamment publié des articles appelant à des réformes démocratiques. En novembre 2005, il a été brièvement libéré, avant d’être de nouveau arrêté deux jours plus tard. Comme Dawit Isaak, Temesgen Ghebreyesus, Seyoum Tsehaye et Amanuel Asrat n’ont jamais été jugés. Depuis, aucune information n’a permis d’établir avec certitude leur lieu de détention ou leur état de santé. Interrogé en 2009 par la chaîne de télévision suédoise TV4 sur la situation de Dawit Isaak, le président du pays, Isaias Afwerki, avait répondu : “Je me fiche de l’endroit où il est ou de ce qu’il fait. Il a fait une grosse erreur” , sans fournir plus d’explications. En décembre 2025, à l’issue de la première visite du gouvernement suédois depuis plus de 30 ans, la ministre des Affaires étrangères Maria Malmer Stenergard avait affirmé à l’ Agence France-Presse ( AFP ) que le journaliste était en vie, selon l’ “évaluation” du ministère. “La détention arbitraire depuis 25 ans de Dawit Isaak et de ses confrères Temesgen Ghebreyesus, Seyoum Tsehaye et Amanuel Asrat, est une tragédie qui n’a que trop duré. Détenus au secret pendant un quart de siècle, en dehors de tout cadre légal, ils subissent une violation grave et manifeste de leurs droits fondamentaux, qui est au cœur de la plainte pour crimes contre l’humanité, déposée par RSF en Suède en 2024, visant le président Isaias Afwerki et d’autres hauts responsables érythréens. Cette longue détention constitue aussi une entrave durable contre le droit des Érythréens à être informés. À l’occasion de ce triste anniversaire et à l’initiative de RSF, 100 journalistes du monde entier lancent un appel à la communauté internationale pour obtenir leur libération et faire toute la lumière sur les circonstances de leur détention. Les responsables de ces actes doivent répondre de leurs responsabilités. Sadibou Marong Directeur du bureau Afrique subsaharienne de RSF Une mobilisation internationale pour sa libération Depuis 2001, les appels à la libération se sont multipliés. En 2016, la Commission africaine des droits de l’homme et des peuples a demandé aux autorités érythréennes de libérer le journaliste ou d'organiser un procès rapide et équitable, et de lui verser des compensations. Le Groupe de travail des Nations unies sur la détention arbitraire a par ailleurs été saisi par une coalition d’avocats et d’organisations, dont RSF, à l’initiative du Centre Raoul Wallenberg pour les droits de la personne. En mars 2023, les experts ont conclu que la détention prolongée de Dawit Isaak violait 19 articles du Pacte international relatif aux droits civils et politiques et de la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme, que le gouvernement a promis d'honorer. Ils avaient alors appelé les autorités érythréennes à “libérer immédiatement et sans condition M. Isaak et lui accorder un droit exécutoire à une indemnisation et à d'autres réparations, conformément au droit international” . En septembre 2024, la section suédoise de RSF a déposé une plainte auprès du parquet suédois visant le président Isaias Afwerki et d’autres hauts responsables érythréens, pour des faits susceptibles de constituer des crimes contre l’humanité, sans obtenir l’ouverture d’une enquête. Une autre plainte de l’organisation avait été introduite dix ans plus tôt. La justice suédoise avait annoncé l’ouverture d’une enquête avant de se rétracter quelques semaines plus tard, estimant qu’au vu du refus prévisible de coopérer de la justice érythréenne, une investigation serait peine perdue . L'Érythrée est l'État qui a occupé le plus souvent le dernier rang du Classement mondial de la liberté de la presse depuis sa création en 2002, devant la Corée du Nord. https://rsf.org/fr/turquie-tu%C4%9Fba-te.body: Turquie : Tuğba Tekerek placée en détention, la liberté de la presse mise à mal dans le cadre d’une répression contre la communauté LGBTQ+ Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Reporters sans frontières (RSF) demande la libération immédiate de la journaliste indépendante Tuğba Tekerek. Elle a été arrêtée dans le cadre de la campagne nationale de perquisitions “Ailem Güvende” (“Ma famille est en sécurité”) visant les organisations LGBTQ+ et est placée en détention provisoire depuis le 15 septembre. Elle fait l’objet d’une enquête pour un article journalistique datant de 2024, publié sur le site d’information Kaos GL, consacré à la communauté LGBTQ+ en Géorgie. Deux reporters qui couvraient les manifestations contre ces perquisitions ont également été placés en garde à vue. RSF considère ces événements comme une nouvelle escalade de la répression contre le journalisme indépendant en Turquie. Le procureur d’Ankara a accusé Tuğba Tekerek de gérer le compte Instagram de l’organisation LGBTQ+ Kaos GL . Cependant, la journaliste a déclaré aux procureurs lors d’un interrogatoire le 15 septembre qu’elle n’avait rédigé qu’un seul article pour le site d’information de cette organisation, également intitulé Kaos GL , en octobre 2024, sur la situation des personnes queer en Géorgie à l’approche des élections législatives dans ce pays, et qu’elle ne s’était même jamais rendue dans les locaux de l’organisation. Le 15 septembre, un tribunal a placé Tuğba Tekerek et sept membres du conseil d’administration de Kaos GL en détention provisoire. Parmi les motifs invoqués pour justifier leur détention figurent des violations présumées de la loi sur les associations et des accusations relatives à des publications “obscènes”. Le site web principal de Kaos GL et son portail d’information ont depuis été bloqués sur décision judiciaire. “Lorsque les droits des minorités sont mis sous pression, la liberté de la presse l’est souvent également. Les récentes attaques contre la communauté LGBTQ+ ont ouvert la voie à une répression étatique plus large, puisque sont pris pour cible ceux qui traitent de sujets jugés par les autorités comme contraires à la conception étatique de la moralité et de la protection de la famille. Lorsque le travail journalistique sur les minorités sociales est criminalisé, c’est en fin de compte toute la population de la Turquie qui est privée de son droit à une information indépendante. Christian Mihr Directeur exécutif de RSF Allemagne Plusieurs journalistes interpellés en l’espace de quelques jours Dans le cadre du plan plus large du gouvernement turc visant à “protéger la famille”, les organisations LGBTQ+, les personnalités publiques et les comptes sur les réseaux sociaux ont été qualifiés de menace pour les structures familiales et ont fait l’objet de mesures répressives sévères. Selon le ministre turc de la Justice, Akın Gürlek, les autorités ont engagé des poursuites judiciaires contre 162 personnes, neuf associations et 13 entreprises dans 15 provinces depuis le 13 septembre. Ces perquisitions et arrestations ont déclenché des manifestations. Le 15 septembre, la police est intervenue lors d’une manifestation devant le tribunal de Çağlayan, à Istanbul, et a placé 109 personnes en garde à vue, dont des journalistes venus couvrir les manifestations. Sarya Toprak , journaliste au quotidien BirGün , et Şener Azak , caméraman au bureau d’Istanbul de la chaîne publique allemande ARD , ont notamment été placés en garde à vue. Tous deux ont été remis en liberté dans les 48 heures suivant leur interpellation. RSF recense depuis des années le recours à la détention préventive et aux poursuites pénales contre les professionnels des médias critiques à l’égard des autorités turques. En mai 2026, RSF avait appelé à la libération des journalistes Alican Uludağ , Merdan Yanardağ et İsmail Arı , qui avaient été placés en détention en raison de leur travail journalistique. Merdan Yanardağ est toujours en détention. RSF a également demandé la relaxe des journalistes poursuivis pour leur couverture des manifestations de masse de mars 2025 . La Turquie occupe la 163e place sur 180 pays dans le Classement mondial de la liberté de la presse 2026 . https://rsf.org/fr/demande-de-libert%C3%.body: Demande de liberté provisoire de Ravi Nair rejetée : le journaliste d’investigation ciblé par un harcèlement judiciaire après ses enquêtes sur le groupe Adani Le journaliste d’investigation Ravi Nair, détenu depuis le 17 sept au Gujarat dans une affaire de diffamation liée au groupe Adani, s’est vu refuser sa libération sous caution. Image:RSF Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Ce 23 septembre, le journaliste d’investigation Ravi Nair s’est vu refuser sa libération, alors qu’il est détenu depuis le 17 septembre dans la prison centrale de Sabarmati, dans l’État du Gujarat pour une affaire de diffamation au pénal déposée par l’entreprise Adani Enterprises Limited. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) alerte sur un acharnement judiciaire contre le journaliste d’investigation, visé par plusieurs procédures judiciaires liées à son travail d’investigation sur le vaste conglomérat indien dirigé par le milliardaire Gautam Adani. Mise à jour du 25/09/26 : Un tribunal de Gandhinagar a accordé une libération sous caution au journaliste le 24 septembre dans l’affaire de diffamation pénale engagée par Adani Enterprises Limited, ouvrant la voie à sa remise en liberté. En Inde, enquêter sur le groupe Adani peut conduire un journaliste en prison. Pour le journaliste d’investigation indépendant Ravi Nair, c’est l'aboutissement d’une affaire qui remonte à septembre 2021, lorsque Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL) a engagé une procédure pénale en diffamation contre lui à propos d’ une série de 17 posts diffusées sur X entre octobre 2020 et juillet 2021. Ces messages relayaient notamment des articles de presse tels ceux du média indépendant NewsClick , du Guardian ou du site indépendant sri-lankais Newsfirst , dont quatre de ses propres enquêtes, et des informations déjà publiques. Le 10 février 2026, un tribunal de Mansa l’a condamné au pénal pour diffamation à un an de prison. Ravi Nair a fait appel devant la haute cour du Gujarat et obtenu, le 9 mars, la suspension de sa peine et sa remise en liberté sous caution. À une audience du 3 septembre, pour laquelle il avait demandé une dispense de comparution pour raisons médicales, le juge a refusé la dispense et émis un mandat d’arrêt sans possibilité de libération sous caution. Le 17 septembre, Ravi Nair s’est présenté en personne devant le tribunal, qui a rejeté sa demande de retrait du mandat d’arrêt et ordonné son incarcération. Le journaliste a saisi la haute cour du Gujarat le 19 septembre pour contester son arrestation et sa détention. Ce mercredi 23 septembre, la haute cour du Gujarat a mis son jugement en délibéré et a rejeté sa demande de libération provisoire. Une nouvelle audience est prévue le 30 septembre 2026 pour examiner sa demande d’annulation du mandat d'arrêt. ““L’arrestation de Ravi Nair alors qu’un appel est en cours contre sa condamnation dans une affaire pénale de diffamation montre de façon choquante comment les lois sont utilisées comme une arme par de puissants intérêts privés pour faire taire le journalisme indépendant. Emprisonner un journaliste d’investigation pour avoir mis sous les projecteurs un conglomérat comme le groupe Adani sur des questions d’intérêt public crée un précédent inquiétant pour la liberté de la presse en Inde. RSF demande aux autorités judiciaires de libérer immédiatement le journaliste victime d’une procédure-bâillon. Le gouvernement indien doit adopter une loi contre les poursuites-bâillons présentant des garanties de nature à empêcher que la diffamation ne puisse être invoquée abusivement devant les tribunaux et conduise à des peines particulièrement sévères. Les journalistes qui enquêtent sur des sujets d'intérêt public doivent être protégés, pas criminalisés. Célia Mercier Responsable du bureau Asie du Sud de RSF Journaliste d'investigation indépendant de 52 ans, Ravi Nair a réalisé de nombreuses enquêtes sur les pratiques commerciales et les liens politiques du groupe Adani. Une grande partie de son travail d’investigation sur le groupe a été publiée sur la plateforme d’investigation Adani Watch . Ses articles ont également été publiés dans des médias tels que le Huffpost , le Leaflet , Frontline et Caravan . Affilié à l’Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), Ravi Nair a participé à une enquête d’août 2023 publiée par le Financial Times et le Guardian , qui révélait que deux investisseurs secrets du groupe Adani avaient des liens étroits avec la famille Adani, soulevant des questions sur d’éventuelles violations de la loi indienne. Plus récemment, en octobre 2025, Ravi Nair a co-réalisé une enquête du Washington Post selon laquelle des responsables indiens auraient rédigé une proposition visant à orienter environ 3,9 milliards de dollars d’investissements de la Life Insurance Corporation of India, une entreprise publique, vers les entreprises du groupe Adani. Ravi Nair est actuellement visé au total par trois procédures en diffamation liées à ses reportages et à ses publications sur les réseaux sociaux concernant le groupe Adani. Ces affaires s’inscrivent dans une offensive judiciaire plus vaste du groupe Adani , documentée par RSF, visant des médias et des journalistes qui enquêtent sur le conglomérat. https://rsf.org/fr/moussa-kaka-disparu-a.body: Moussa Kaka, disparu au Niger : quatre décennies de journalisme et de combat pour la liberté de la presse Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Moussa Kaka est une figure du journalisme au Sahel. Celui qui a disparu depuis le 31 août raconte le Niger depuis près de 40 ans, notamment au sein de la radio qu’il a lancée, Radio Saraounia. C’est un témoin privilégié de la vie de son pays et du Sahel. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) retrace le parcours de ce journaliste chevronné et réaffirme son appel aux autorités du Niger à ouvrir une enquête. Quand on le retrouve sur le terrain, à Niamey, la capitale du Niger, ou dans les autres localités du pays, Moussa Kaka échange volontiers, donne des conseils et encourage les plus jeunes qui ont choisi le métier qu’ils aiment : le journalisme. Ainsi va la vie de ce journaliste de renom, disparu depuis le 31 août dernier après avoir quitté son bureau en fin de journée pour regagner son domicile, mais n’y est jamais arrivé. Raconter en profondeur le Niger, vaste pays de près de 1,27 million de kilomètres carrés, frontalier de sept autres pays dont le Mali et le Burkina Faso, a toujours été le sacerdoce de ce “baroudeur de l’information”, sillonnant souvent les vastes étendues désertiques du Sahara, traversant les hameaux les plus reculés, ou même fréquentant les salles de réunion des hôtels de la capitale, pour collecter des informations. “Là où beaucoup de journalistes hésitaient souvent pour leur sécurité, Moussa a toujours été sur le terrain dans les centres urbains comme dans le désert au moment des conflits armés,” témoigne un doyen de la presse nigérienne. À plus de 66 ans, fort de 40 années de pratique journalistique, Moussa Kaka est celui qui était toujours sur “l'actualité chaude”, raconte un journaliste de sa génération. Il a couvert évènements, conflits, dialogue et plusieurs aspects de ce territoire au nom du droit des populations sahéliennes à l’information. “Par son métier, Moussa Kaka a toujours eu des contacts avec toutes les couches de la société ; avec les différents hommes politiques, la société civile, et les mouvements armés et l'armée, au point que beaucoup s'interrogent sur pourquoi lui et pas les autres”, explique un journaliste. Il a commencé sa carrière à la radio nationale du Niger, puis a créé en 1999 Radio Saraounia , qui sera suivie en 2011 de la chaîne de télévision du même nom. Moussa Kaka se retrouve à la tête d’un groupe de presse de 70 personnes dont 35 à Niamey. Le groupe a des antennes entre autres, dans les régions de Tahoua, Maradi et Madaoua. Moussa Kaka a aussi raconté le Niger à l’international. Il a été correspondant pour Radio France Internationale ( RFI ) jusqu’en 2023 – année à laquelle ce média a été suspendu par les autorités militaires.Il a également fait partie des correspondants de RSF, documentant les violations de la liberté de la presse et se mobilisant pour la protection de ses confrères. Porté disparu après un putsch avorté... Depuis le 31 août 2026, après qu’il s’est mis en route, vers 19 heures, pour rentrer chez lui, Moussa Kaka n'a plus donné signe de vie. Les autorités du Niger n’ont, à ce jour, ni déclaré publiquement avoir ouvert une enquête ni communiqué sur sa disparition, intervenue dans un contexte particulièrement tendu, quelques jours après la tentative avortée de coup d’État du 29 août à Niamey. “Cette disparition, depuis près d’un mois, envoie des signaux inquiétants aux acteurs de la presse du pays qui s'efforcent d’exercer un journalisme indépendant, loin de la propagande, avec courage et résilience. La mobilisation de tous, en premier lieu des autorités, est nécessaire pour retrouver Moussa Kaka et lui permettre de retrouver sa famille, ses collègues et reprendre son travail. Sadibou Marong Directeur du bureau Afrique subsaharienne de RSF Certains de ses confrères décrivent Moussa Kaka comme faisant partie d’un groupe de journalistes parmi les plus persécutés ces dernières années. Entre septembre 2007 et octobre 2008, il a d’ailleurs passé 384 jours derrière les barreaux, pour une accusation contestée d’“acte de nature à nuire à la défense nationale”. Les pressions n’avaient jamais cessé pour celui qui est décrit par Harouna Ibrahim, ancien président de la Maison de la presse de Niamey, comme “un journaliste ayant connu beaucoup de difficultés dans [leur] pays”. En octobre 2025, Moussa Kaka avait été interpellé , ainsi que cinq autres journalistes, après avoir annoncé sur les réseaux sociaux une conférence de presse au sujet d’un fonds de solidarité créé par le gouvernement pour lever des fonds pour soutenir les opérations des forces de sécurité de l’État. Les autorités les avaient inculpés de “complicité de diffusion de document de nature à troubler l'ordre public” en vertu de la loi sur la cybercriminalité. La constance professionnelle de Moussa Kaka, malgré les persécutions, fait consensus. “ C’est un professionnel rigoureux qui travaille dans le respect de l'éthique et la déontologie du métier", conclut Harouna Ibrahim. https://rsf.org/fr/cuba-face-aux-coupure.body: Cuba : face aux coupures prolongées, RSF déploie une aide d’urgence pour assurer l’alimentation électrique et la connectivité de la presse indépendante Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel L’aggravation de la crise énergétique à Cuba constitue un obstacle supplémentaire pour les journalistes, dans un pays où l’exercice indépendant de la profession reste soumis à de sévères restrictions. Alors que les pannes du réseau électrique perturbent les communications à travers le pays, Reporters sans frontières (RSF) apporte son soutien aux professionnels indépendants affectés, afin de leur permettre de maintenir un accès minimal à l’énergie et à la connectivité et de poursuivre leur travail d’information. Le 18 septembre, le réseau électrique cubain a été frappé par une nouvelle panne généralisée, privant des millions de personnes d’électricité. Ces dernières semaines, certaines zones de La Havane ont connu des coupures de plus de 30 heures, tandis que la situation s’est avérée plus critique dans plusieurs provinces. “Tout devient très difficile lorsqu’on n’a pas d’électricité. La vie change complètement, car les habitudes et les horaires de travail sont bouleversés” , témoigne auprès de RSF un journaliste indépendant cubain, dont l’identité est tenue secrète pour des raisons de sécurité. L’absence d’électricité complique le rechargement des téléphones, ordinateurs, appareils photo et autres équipements indispensables. Elle perturbe également l’accès à Internet, les échanges avec les sources et la transmission des informations. Pour en limiter les conséquences, RSF fournit aux journalistes présents sur l’île des solutions d’alimentation électrique et de connectivité alternatives. “Ce soutien me permet de garantir que je puisse terminer mon travail”, t émoigne l’un des bénéficiaires . “Pour les journalistes indépendants à Cuba, la crise énergétique ne se résume pas à la seule question de l’accès à l’électricité. Les coupures entravent directement leur capacité à communiquer, à accéder à l’information et à documenter la situation sur l’île. Dans un contexte où ils sont déjà confrontés à de sévères restrictions, à la surveillance et aux intimidations, leur garantir un accès minimal à l’énergie et à la connectivité est essentiel pour permettre le maintien d’un journalisme indépendant. Artur Romeu Directeur du bureau Amérique latine de RSF La crise énergétique vient encore fragiliser un environnement médiatique déjà très contraint à Cuba. L’État y conserve un contrôle étroit du paysage médiatique, tandis que les journalistes indépendants font face à de nombreuses restrictions. La combinaison des coupures d’électricité, d’un accès limité à Internet et des pressions exercées sur la presse risque de compliquer davantage leur travail, notamment pour documenter les conséquences de la crise et permettre au public d’accéder à une information indépendante. Dans son Classement mondial de la liberté de la presse 2026, RSF place Cuba au 160e rang sur 180 pays. https://www.rferl.org/a/kyrgyzstan-iraq-.body: Kyrgyzstan Kyrgyz Families Plead For Return Of Islamic State Fighters' Wives, Relatives From Iraqi Prisons By Datkabek Shabdanbek Uulu and Farangis Najibullah September 19, 2026 15:17 CET Kyrgyz Families Plead For Return Of Islamic State Fighters' Wives, Relatives From Iraqi Prisons Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A Kyrgyz humanitarian worker at Bishkek airport holds a child who was among 79 children repatriated from Iraq in 2021. (file photo.) Listen to this article 4 min This audio is automated Learn more Just over 12 years ago, Kamaldin Teshebaev and his wife had a large family of three sons, three daughters-in-law, and 16 grandchildren. They lived a stable, working-class life in the small town of Kyzyl-Kiya in southwestern Kyrgyzstan. But the traditional Kyrgyz family’s world came crashing down when one of his sons -- a migrant worker in Russia left for Syria in 2014 along with his own family, to join Islamic State (IS) as the extremist group gained a foothold there. Soon, the other brothers followed suit. Teshebaev, who is in his 70s, says his three sons and three of his grandchildren were killed in Syria. After IS lost the territory it controlled in Iraq and Syria, tens of thousands of foreign fighters and their family members were detained or placed in camps. In Iraq, many foreign women who had traveled to live under IS, including wives of IS militants, were subsequently convicted under the country’s counterterrorism laws. Teshebaev’s daughters-in-law also ended up in Iraqi prisons after the collapse of IS's self-proclaimed caliphate. Teshebaev says his wife traveled to Syria to try to “bring them back,” but she ended up in an Iraqi prison too. Details of her case could not be independently verified, but her family says she is also being held on charges linked to terrorism. “I am alone now, but I am grateful to our president and government that brought back my grandchildren,” Teshebaev said. “They are grown up now, two of them recently got married.” His 13 surviving grandchildren were among 79 children of Kyrgyz IS fighters whom Bishkek repatriated from Iraq in a humanitarian operation in 2021. SEE ALSO: The Women Who Came Home: Kazakhstan Tries To Rehabilitate Islamic State Returnees Kyrgyzstan and other Central Asian states have organized similar missions, coordinating with local authorities and international organizations to repatriate some of their nationals, primarily women and children. Fresh Hope For Repatriation Teshebaev joined dozens of people who gathered outside Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov’s office on September 14 to appeal for the return of family members still imprisoned in Iraq. According to Kyrgyz authorities, 41 Kyrgyz citizens are currently being held in Iraqi prisons. Most of them are the wives or relatives of IS fighters. Relatives who have long campaigned for their families’ repatriation, have now been given fresh hope. In August, Iraq's Justice Ministry announced it was considering transferring nearly 6,000 foreign nationals detained over links to IS back to their home countries. SEE ALSO: Grandmother Raises An Orphan Of Islamic State, As Kazakhs Confront Reintegration Question Teshebaev says his wife and daughters-in-law call him from Iraq, saying that they are desperate to return home and serve their sentences in Kyrgyzstan. Kyrgyz authorities had not responded to the families’ appeal by the time this report was published. 'I Am In Great Pain' Among those appealing for help was Rahima Niyzamova, whose 41-year-old daughter, Zebo Alieva, has been held at Iraq’s Rusafa prison for more than eight years. Alieva had been working in Turkey in 2015 when her husband -- an IS fighter -- convinced her to move to Iraq to join him, her mother says. Niyzamova has been raising her daughter's four children who were brought back home by the Kyrgyz government in 2021. "I am in great pain. Just imagine, a mother's child is sitting in prison. I’ve developed diabetes, and a heart condition,” she said. Niyzamova said her daughter's youngest child was only eight months old when she was imprisoned. The child is now nine. Farangis Najibullah Farangis Najibullah is a senior correspondent for RFE/RL who has reported on a wide range of topics from Central Asia, including the impact of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on the region. She has extensively covered efforts by Central Asian states to repatriate and reintegrate their citizens who joined Islamic State in Syria and Iraq. This item is part of Features Iraq Kyrgyzstan

https://www.rferl.org/a/tripp-azerbaijan.body: News US Set To Unveil Next Steps for Trump-Backed Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Corridor By Alex Raufoglu September 23, 2026 13:58 CET US Set To Unveil Next Steps for Trump-Backed Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Corridor Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (left) and Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan after signing an agreement related to the TRIPP project in Yerevan in May. NEW YORK, United States -- The United States is set to unveil the next stage of its effort to develop the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP, a planned transport and infrastructure corridor through southern Armenia that Washington says could open new trade routes between the South Caucasus, Central Asia, and Western markets. Senior State Department officials told reporters that the New York event on September 23 will focus on the institutional and financial mechanisms needed to move TRIPP from last year's Armenia-Azerbaijan peace initiative toward implementation. The event is expected to bring together the foreign ministers of Armenia and Azerbaijan, representatives of the five Central Asian states -- with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan showing particular interest -- US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Republican Senator Steve Daines, and executives from more than 40 companies, many of them American. Officials said the event will highlight how TRIPP aims to "pop the cork" on the Middle Corridor, unlocking a westward trade route that connects Europe to Central Asia while reducing reliance on transit through Russia, China, and Iran. Map: Proposed Trump Route For International Peace And Prosperity (TRIPP) The gathering will also feature the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund, which officials said will invest in opportunities arising from TRIPP and the wider Trans-Caspian trade route. The fund operates at arm's length from the US government under a White House-appointed board and receives grant funding from the State Department. It is distinct from the TRIPP Development Company, the joint US-Armenian corporate entity being established to develop and oversee the corridor. 'A Major Security Issue' TRIPP is intended to provide unimpeded access between Azerbaijan proper and its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory while respecting Armenia's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security. "This becomes a major security issue for us," the official said, describing the removal of existing trade "choke points" as a central objective. The transit route will be developed and managed by a US-controlled company, giving Washington exclusive rights while effectively excluding Russia from a strategically important project in one of its traditional spheres of influence. SEE ALSO: Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape The project emerged from an August 2025 White House summit at which Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a US-brokered joint declaration aimed at ending decades of conflict between the two South Caucasus neighbors. Armenia and Azerbaijan fought two major wars over Nagorno-Karabakh, an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that for decades had a predominantly ethnic-Armenian population. Azerbaijan regained full control of the territory in 2023, prompting almost all of its ethnic Armenia population to flee. The two sides agreed on the text of a peace treaty in March 2025, but a final agreement has yet to be completed. Officials said there have been no cease-fire violations since the August summit and pointed to limited trade in fuel and agricultural products as evidence of growing economic integration. According to them, Azerbaijani fuel supplies have contributed to an estimated 20 to 30 percent decline in Armenian fuel costs. They noted there had been more interaction between Washington and Baku during the previous 13 to 14 months than during the preceding 13 to 14 years. A senior State Department official said Yerevan and Baku were acting as though peace were "inevitable," although additional steps remain before a final agreement can be completed. Washington intends to develop TRIPP in parallel with that process, arguing that greater economic integration could help remove remaining obstacles. Physical Construction Still Some Way Off Despite plans to move TRIPP toward implementation, construction of the roughly 43-kilometer section through Armenia is not yet ready to begin. The section is expected to include a railway, road, pipelines, electricity infrastructure, and digital data links. The senior State Department official said Azerbaijan has already been building infrastructure toward the Armenian border at its own expense, while Turkey is similarly developing infrastructure up to the border. The remaining section through Armenia is still to be developed. “We're not there yet,” the official said when asked how soon physical construction of the Armenian section could begin. The administration hopes to begin looking for business and investment opportunities by the end of 2026 or the first quarter of 2027. SEE ALSO: US Congressman Abraham Hamadeh: Armenia-Azerbaijan Peace Deal Could Come Before Trump's Term Ends The railway will take longer. A feasibility study is expected by the end of 2026 or early 2027, after which companies will be able to bid. The official said completing the railway would likely take at least 18 months, complicated by difficult topography. Electricity connections could come sooner. Discussions are already underway, with officials expecting electricity operations to begin in 2027, potentially linking the Armenian and Azerbaijani grids with wider Central Asia, Turkish, and European regional networks. Passenger rail is also planned. TRIPP Leadership The briefers provided more detail about the planned structure of the TRIPP Development Company (TDC) but no names for its future leadership. The TDC is being established as a corporate joint venture between the US government and Armenia. The senior State Department official described it as a first-of-its-kind arrangement in which the US will hold a majority stake, with its own board, voting procedures, and management. Several legal matters still need to be finalized before the company can formally be announced. Projects involving rail, roads, electricity, oil, gas, and data will go through regular tender processes for construction or concessions. The US Development Finance Corporation (DFC) has been involved in the legal and institutional setup, but the TDC itself will operate as a separate US-Armenian corporate entity. The United States is prepared to invest once feasibility studies establish that individual projects are commercially viable. The State Department is financing part of the feasibility work, with engineering firm AECOM set to present investors with projects unlocked by TRIPP during the event on September 23. 'A Difficult Neighborhood' Officials described TRIPP as an alternative to existing east-west routes, with the proposed corridor offering Central Asian trade another route to Western markets that bypasses Russia and Iran. SEE ALSO: Russia Uses Economic Chokehold To Counter Armenia's Westward Tilt The senior State Department official said Washington had held discussions with regional competitors but declined to characterize their private views. "There have been numerous conversations with all of the competitors in the region," the official said, adding that Washington was aware of the potential for "hard conversations" in what officials called a difficult neighborhood. The event is intended to mark a shift from the 2025 peace initiative toward implementation, with more than 40 companies attending. https://www.rferl.org/a/georgia-french-e.body: Photo Galleries New Georgian Publication Captures The Caucasus As It Was, Two Centuries Ago September 27, 2026 11:19 CET By Eka Kevanishvili Photo: Public domain Photo Galleries New Georgian Publication Captures The Caucasus As It Was, Two Centuries Ago September 27, 2026 11:19 CET By Eka Kevanishvili New Georgian Publication Captures The Caucasus As It Was, Two Centuries Ago Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Two hundred years after the publication of a French book that captured life in the Caucasus in the early 1800s, the work has been published in the Georgian language for the first time. Journey Through Southern Russia was produced by Jacques Francois Gamba (1763-1833), who was the first French consul in Georgia -- then part of the Russian Empire. A view of the Sukhumi Fortress in Abkhazia in the early 1800s. The landmark is now ruins. The traveler and merchant first published his accounts of his journeys through Georgia and the Caucasus in France in 1824–1826, in two volumes accompanied by an album of maps and illustrations. The sketches inside the album are not credited but most are believed to have been made by the French-Russian explorer-artist Jean-Marie Chopin. A sketch of the Surami Fortress, near Gori. The Surami fortress seen in 2004. Gamba made two trips to the Russian empire in the early 1800s, largely to explore potential trading opportunities for Paris. “Gamba is not just a traveler who passed through here,” Sulkhan Saladze, the publisher of the Georgian-language version of the Frenchman's masterpiece, told RFE/RL’s Georgian Service at the book’s September 24 launch. “He stayed in Tbilisi for a long time -- that enabled this view of the vibrant everyday life of the city, which had not changed since the days of [18th century monarch] Heraclius II.” Women depicted dancing in Tbilisi. “His journey [to the Caucasus] reflects the kinds of interests France had here at the time, and what the arrival of French capital in Tbilisi might have led to if everything had gone as the French had envisaged,” Saladze says. “But, during Gamba’s diplomatic mission, the Russian Empire was already becoming dominant here, they were the principal player and blocked everything,” the publisher notes. A grape seller from the Mingrelia Region. Gamba’s mission was to describe the region’s economic life and the prospects for developing trade. But his reports explored beyond those themes to relay history and culture of the region to his French audience, and Tbilisi’s potential future . “When trade here develops to its full potential, [Uzbeks] coming from Samarkand, Tibet, and the borders of China, will meet Hindu merchants from Lahore and Gujarat in Tbilisi’s markets.” A view over Tbilisi from the southern hills of the city showing the Narikala Fortress (left) and the Kura River. A view over Tbilisi as it looked in 2021. “At times merchants from Paris, couriers from St. Petersburg, traders from Constantinople, Englishmen from Calcutta and Madras, and finally Armenians from Smyrna and Yazd, and Uzbeks from Bukhara, all arrive in Tbilisi at the same time,” Gamba observed. “Therefore this city may be regarded as a key point between Europe and Asia." Gamba passed away in Tbilisi in 1833 but his burial place is unknown. Amos Chapple and Sindre Langmoen contributed to this report New Georgian Publication Captures The Caucasus As It Was, Two Centuries Ago Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print Eka Kevanishvili Eka Kevanishvili is a correspondent in Tbilisi for RFE/RL's Georgian Service. https://www.rferl.org/a/zelenskyy-drones.body: News Russian Strikes On Ukraine As Zelenskyy Says Russia Not Ready To End War By RFE/RL September 27, 2026 00:00 CET Updated September 27, 2026 10:17 CET Russian Strikes On Ukraine As Zelenskyy Says Russia Not Ready To End War Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy Listen to this article 6 min This audio is automated Learn more Russian drone strikes killed at least four people in Ukraine overnight and into September 27, including one person in the capital, Kyiv, and three in the southeastern Zaporizhzhya region, Ukrainian officials said. In Kyiv, a man was killed when a Russian drone struck a nonresidential building in the Solomyansky district, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. A fire broke out at a car-repair facility in the same district, while another nonresidential building was hit, the agency said. It shared images showing firefighters battling fires at the damaged buildings. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a Russian strike on the Shevchenkivsky district injured a woman and two 16-year-old children. The three were hospitalized, he said. In the Zaporizhzhya region in the country's southeast , three people were killed in Russian strikes, according to the regional military administration. A man was killed in the village of Komyshuvakha, where one house was destroyed and several others damaged, it said. Two more people, a man and a woman, were killed when a Russian strike hit their car in the village of Novotavriyske. Four people were also wounded in the attack on Komyshuvakha, the administration said. Trump Tells Kyiv To 'Settle' War Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has declined to confirm that he had agreed to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's statement on September 25 that Trump had made a “final decision” to grant Kyiv a license to produce the air-defense missiles. Asked about the Patriot agreement on September 26, Trump said he wanted Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin to “settle” their war. Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on September 22. “We talked about a lot of different subjects, and many of those subjects...very strong agreement,” Trump told reporters about the meeting. “But you know what I want him to do? Make a deal. I want him to settle with Putin, and I want Putin to settle with him.” Zelenskyy said after the meeting that he hoped Washington would help end the war “as soon as possible.” He has also called on Trump to maintain pressure on Moscow, including through new sanctions. Zelenskyy: Putin Seeks Excuses To Keep Fighting In his latest nightly video address, Zelenskyy said Moscow is showing no signs it is ready to end its war on its neighbor and he called on the West to remain united in efforts to force the Kremlin to the negotiating table. “Obviously, the Russians are not preparing to stop their war, at least for now,” Zelenskyy said, citing intelligence reports that Moscow is intending to hike spending on deadly jet-powered drones and other munitions. Putin “always finds some lame excuse -- not to meet, not to hold a trilateral, not to talk, not to end it, not to stop the killing.” Embed share Geran-4 Unpacked: What Makes Russia's New Jet-Powered Drone So Dangerous? by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:04:12 0:00 “It has been the same with him for years – and all our partners feel it. He is looking for excuses to keep waging the war. It always sounds the same -- and our recent meeting with the US president showed that,” Zelenskyy added in the September 26 address. 'Expand Their War' The Ukrainian leader claimed that Russia plans to spend $12 billion in the upcoming year on the production of “jet-powered drones and loitering munitions alone -- just on this one category of weapons.” “This directly concerns our partners as well. Many intelligence services have information that the Russians want to expand their war, their activities, to more countries. Perhaps to other regions. That is why we need to build our defense together. That is why we need to defend ourselves together, preventively.” ⁠He said Ukrainian ⁠air defenses have been able to intercept 55 percent of jet-powered drones ⁠launched by Russia as overnight attacks on Kyiv and other cities have become increasingly frequent as cold weather starts to set in. “We are working on this together -- with America, with Europe, with Canada, with Japan, and with many others around the world who are helping us, helping Ukraine, helping our people,” he added. Zelenskyy wrote on social media that “we ask President Trump to implement the Lindsey Graham Act against Russia and everyone who props up its war financially." SEE ALSO: Zelenskyy Calls On Trump To Enact Russia Sanctions After Deadly Attacks Across Ukraine The law, signed by Trump a week ago, gives the president sweeping new authority to impose sanctions and tariffs on Russia, its energy sector, and foreign governments and entities that help Moscow evade existing restrictions. The Ukrainian president told journalists in New York that Washington had proposed holding what would be the first Ukraine-Russia-US meeting in many months at a relatively low "technical level," with the United Arab Emirates serving as host. While there was no immediate confirmation from the United States, Putin said that all peace proposals were "on the table" but added that Moscow had to weigh its interests. More Infrastructure Hit French news agency AFP said an analysis of data from a leading conflict monitor indicate a significant increase in strikes against Ukraine's infrastructure over recent months. It said figures compiled by the Armed Conflict Location and Event ( ACLED ) show Russia has struck twice as many warehouses in the Kyiv region over the past three months as in all previous years of the war combined. ACLED recorded some 100 strikes or series of strikes on civilian storage facilities in the Kyiv region since mid-June, up from just 50 between February 2022 and mid-June of of this year. https://www.rferl.org/a/afghanistan-iran.body: Afghanistan An Afghan Mother And Her Daughters Left Their Homeland In Search Of A Better Life. They Died Of Thirst By RFE/RL's Radio Azadi September 23, 2026 14:30 CET An Afghan Mother And Her Daughters Left Their Homeland In Search Of A Better Life. They Died Of Thirst Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Afghan refugees deported from Iran return to their homeland. (file photo) When Nizam Hematkhil heard the news, he rushed to a remote corner of Iran near the border with Pakistan. A group of illegal migrants from Afghanistan had died in Iran’s southeastern province of Sistan-Baluchistan. When Hematkhil arrived in the village of Mak Sukhteh, he found the bodies of his stepmother and her four daughters. “The cause of their deaths was thirst,” Hematkhil told RFE/RL’s Radio Azadi. “I personally recovered their bodies.” They were among the 17 Afghans who died of extreme dehydration in mid-September after crossing Iran through Pakistan, according to foreign-based Iranian human rights group Haalvsh . The deaths have highlighted the dangers faced by Afghan migrants and refugees who risk crossing illegally into Iran to escape extreme poverty and the Taliban’s repressive rule. Locator map: Sistan-Baluchistan, Iran and Balochistan, Pakistan Escaping Extreme Poverty Hematkhil’s stepmother and her daughters, who were aged between six and 15, had been on their way to join him in Iran. The family had all moved to Iran in search of a better life, but most of them returned to Afghanistan last year. “Instead of finding a way to start over, we exhausted all our savings and resources," said Hematkhil, whose family are from the northern Afghan province of Baghlan. “There was little work and no realistic way for the family to support themselves.” “Consequently, they were compelled to return to Iran to survive, as there was practically no other option left," he added. The Taliban’s seizure of power in 2021 worsened one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. Without international development assistance, the Afghan economy has further shrunk as joblessness and poverty rise. Meanwhile, the hard-line Islamist group has committed gross human rights violations, including extrajudicial killings and torture, leading to an exodus to neighboring countries. Embed share Five Afghan Family Members Die Of Thirst While Trying To Reach Iran by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:20 0:00 Critical Condition Hematkhil’s stepmother and her young girls had crossed into Iran without taking water with them, said a relative who accompanied them on the journey. Hematkhil’s stepmother's son, who was also with them, survived. "The son was in critical condition. He had left the women behind," the relative said. "Locals transported him to [the Iranian town of] Saravan, and fortunately, he is doing well." A Taliban diplomatic source confirmed to Radio Azadi that a mother and her four daughters died on September 11 due to severe thirst while crossing Iran. But the source disputed Haalvash’s claim that 17 Afghans had died. Haalvsh released a video appearing to show locals digging graves. Another video purportedly shows people listening to a sermon in Pashto, one of Afghanistan’s two main languages. SEE ALSO: The Iranian Border Is Increasingly Deadly For Afghans Deadly Routes For decades, millions of Afghans fleeing war, persecution, and poverty have sought refuge in Iran. Hundreds of thousands more have moved to the Islamic republic since 2021. The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, estimates that around 4.5 million Afghans live in Iran, including more than 2 million undocumented migrants. Many undocumented Afghans pay traffickers to smuggle them into Iran. The journey is arduous, and migrants often have to cross remote stretches of desert and mountains where food and water are scarce. In July, the bodies of 14 Afghan migrants were found in a desert in southeastern Afghanistan near the border with Iran. The group was believed to have been attempting to cross illegally into Iran. Similar cases have been reported in the past, with migrants dying after running out of water or food. Embed share Iranian Film Casts Real Refugees To Show Plight Of Displaced Afghans by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:04:13 0:00 Crossing the 921-kilometer-long border has become increasingly dangerous for many Afghans as Iran violently cracks down on illegal migrants. At least 10 Afghans were shot dead by Iranian border guards in December, according to Taliban officials, after they entered Iran illegally from western Afghanistan's Farah Province. Seven others were shot dead by border guards in November. The incidents underscore the risks Afghans are willing to take to escape poverty and the dire economic situation in their country. "They think about their futures, believing that if they reach Iran, they can at least find work and earn an income to provide a better life for their families,” Sefatullah Zahedi, a Germany-based migrant rights activist, told Radio Azadi. https://www.rferl.org/a/afghan-refugee-c.body: Afghanistan As Deadline Looms, Ex-US Marine Desperately Seeks Brother At Afghan Refugee Camp In Qatar By Ray Furlong and RFE/RL's Radio Azadi September 25, 2026 12:26 CET As Deadline Looms, Ex-US Marine Desperately Seeks Brother At Afghan Refugee Camp In Qatar Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Sean Jamshidi is pictured during an operation to welcome evacuated Afghan children to the United States at a military base in Quantico, Virginia, in 2021. Mohammad Masood Jamshidi was a security guard at the US consulate in Herat when it was attacked by Taliban bombers . He hoped to get asylum in the United States but now fears deportation to the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). His brother, former US Marine Sean Jamshidi, recently arrived in Qatar, where Masood is being held at a camp along with some 1,100 other Afghans. To Sean's surprise, he was denied access and has spent the past few days desperately trying to reach someone who will let him in. The As-Sayliyah camp , a former US Army base, is due to close on September 30, and its residents still don't know what will happen next. "They're traumatized from this situation, and I want to come and see them and to bring them a little bit of cash," Sean told RFE/RL on September 23, referring to his brother's family. SEE ALSO: 25 Years After 9/11, Could Afghanistan Again Become A Launchpad For Global Terror? "We don't know where they could be relocated to. They keep talking about a third country that's not the United States, maybe in Africa, like the DRC... When I came here, they told me they declined access for me to be able to come on the camp," Sean said. During a previous trip, in February, he was granted access. Fighting For Freedom Many of the Afghans at the camp worked for US forces during the US-led international military presence in Afghanistan between 2001-2021. The others are primarily their family members. Evacuated from the country after the withdrawal of US and international forces in 2021 , they had expected to be welcomed in the United States. But all immigration requests relating to Afghanistan were halted by a presidential executive order in November 2025 after an Afghan national shot two members of the National Guard , one of whom died a day after the shooting near the White House in Washington, D.C. SEE ALSO: Five Years After Fleeing Taliban Rule, At-Risk Afghans Live In Hiding In Pakistan An official at the US State Department told RFE/RL that the United States has "kept its promise to Afghans who risked their lives to support the US government during our attempts to help Afghans build a better country for themselves," adding that roughly 400,000 Afghans have been resettled since 2001. "The State Department continues to work toward a positive resolution that provides safety for these remaining people to start a new life outside of Afghanistan while upholding the safety and security of the American people," the official maintained. However, the official said that "it is long past time to move past this decades-long conflict, and look ahead to the future." According to AfghanEvac , a charity that has helped resettled Afghans who aided the US effort in Afghanistan, 292 resident of the camp have officially been denied access to the United States. It adds that more than 400 camp residents are children. Sean was born in Afghanistan and came to the United States, aged 4, in 2000. He signed up to join the Marine Corps when he turned 18. "I saw the Marines in Afghanistan, I said, 'You know what? I want to be a Marine, stand up for what's right and fight for freedoms, the freedoms that we have in America,'" he said. Across a 10-year stint, Sean served as a commander of security at the US embassy in the DRC and was also involved in caring for evacuated Afghans who reached the United States in 2021. He said his brother, 49-year-old Masood, worked as a security officer for a private contractor at the US consulate in Herat, western Afghanistan, protecting government and diplomatic personnel. Mohammad Masood Jamshidi, right, during his service at the US consulate in Herat. Also pictured is the then US ambassador, James Cunningham. A photo from 2013 shows Masood with the US ambassador at the time, James Cunningham. Also visible is the US seal damaged in a truck bomb attack on the consulate that killed eight Afghan guards in September that year. "The fear and loss would have deterred most individuals from returning, but Mr. Jamshidy (sic) demonstrated his courage and commitment by returning a couple of weeks later," his supervisor wrote in a letter recommending him for a US entry visa in December that year. Masood has been at As-Sayliyah for two years now, along with his wife, three children, son-in-law, and 3-year-old grandchild. "He risked his life. So it's definitely sad that they're talking about a third country when an individual like him literally risked his life for our policies, for our cultural values, for our freedom," Sean said. 'Welcome To The United States' The fate of the people at the camp has been raised at Congressional hearings. In June, Democratic Senator Chris Coons from Delaware said they included "400 children and 150 family members of currently serving active-duty US service members." Responding, Secretary of State Marco Rubio cited the executive order but said Washington had talked with "multiple countries" about giving the Afghans refuge. He said he wanted them to find "the right places to go." The State Department official who commented to RFE/RL called As-Saylilah "a legacy of the Biden Administration’s attempt to move as many Afghans to America as possible without properly vetting them." Physical conditions at the camp are not said to be an issue. But people there have told RFE/RL's Radio Azadi of the frustration of being in limbo for so long and the emotional strain caused by the uncertainty ahead of the September 30 deadline for closure. "Everyone here in the camp is anxious. We are all wondering what will happen to us and what our future will be," one camp inmate, a man who declined to be named, told RFE/RL. Masood Jamshidi, left, during his service at the US consulate in Herat "We cannot trust these people. Will they take us to America, or will they send us to another country -- perhaps somewhere in Africa?" he continued. The man said his family had been scattered by the chaos of war and international politics since the Taliban recaptured Kabul in 2021. Two of his children were in the United States, he said, while a daughter was in Iran and two other children in Afghanistan. "They call us constantly and ask what is happening. They are living in hiding in a house in Kabul. That alone is a source of enormous worry. And then there is our situation here. We sold everything we had -- our home, our belongings and everything else...because we believed we were going to America," the man said. A man who chose to be identified only by his first name, 42-year-old Faraidoon, said the camp authorities held regular meetings with inmates but "at every meeting, they say there is no information." Faraidoon has been in the camp for "about two years" with his wife and three children. "When we arrived, there was even a sign inside the camp saying, 'Welcome to the United States of America.' Now they have simply isolated us, and we do not understand what is happening," he said. SEE ALSO: Sullivan: U.S. Expects 'Safe Passage' For Americans, Afghans From Afghanistan "Yesterday, we had a meeting with the head of the camp and other officials. We asked many questions, but nothing is clear. They told us they have not yet received any order saying that the camp will close on that date. Nor has anyone told us anything about a third country," a 65-year-old inmate said on September 23. Accounts such as these are typical for people in As-Sayliyah. The State Department official told RFE/RL that US authoriti

https://www.rferl.org/a/arashan-giant-sh.body: Kyrgyzstan 'Million Dollar' Mutton: Kyrgyzstan's New Monster Sheep Breed September 24, 2026 15:28 CET By Amos Chapple Photo: Arashan.kz (Courtesy Image) Kyrgyzstan 'Million Dollar' Mutton: Kyrgyzstan's New Monster Sheep Breed September 24, 2026 15:28 CET By Amos Chapple 'Million Dollar' Mutton: Kyrgyzstan's New Monster Sheep Breed Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A new Kyrgyz sheep breed is sparking a speculative frenzy across Central Asia, where rams are changing hands for extraordinary sums. The Arashan breed was officially registered in Kyrgyzstan in April 2021 . Since then, prices have soared as images of the variety's giant rams have gone viral on social media. In 2023 a single Arashan breeding ram was sold for $150,000 , and prices have reportedly climbed since. At a sheep fair in April, a young ram was "valued" at $500,000, and after a September 19 event near Bishkek reports emerged that a Kyrgyz-raised Arashan lamb had recently been sold to a Kazakh breeder for $1 million. An image shared on the Arashan.kz Instagram page in December 2025 features an Arashan sheep named President. "The lamb that sold for $1 million is called Antibiotic," Kyrgyz sheep farmer Ulan Atabaev , who claimed to know the breeders involved in the reported deal, told RFE/RL. The Kazakhstan-based buyer of the prized lamb passed questions from RFE/RL on to a lawyer who said only that "Antibiotic was sold to breeder Kuanysh Myktybayev for a substantial sum." Mirlan Satybekov , chairman of the Kyrgyz Public Association of Sheep Breeders, told RFE/RL the Arashan breed's value comes from their size, rapid growth, and hardiness demanded by the harsh climate and landscape of Kyrgyzstan. "On top of that, they are just very beautiful sheep," Satybekov said. Arashans of valuable bloodlines feature prominent "Roman noses," long ears, and wobbly, fat-filled tails. The sheep are raised for their meat, with lamb and mutton being staples of Central Asian diets. An Arashan sheep at a fair in Kyrgyzstan. The sheep are one of the world's fat-tailed variety, that store pouches of fatty tissue above the hind legs. The animals can draw from the fatty deposits when fodder is scarce. Satybekov told RFE/RL that giant specimens of Arashan breeding rams are used as "improvers" to increase the size and subsequent market value of the next generation of sheep flocks. Farmers pay substantial fees to owners of famed Arashan rams to inseminate their ewes. Additionally, young males from a famous father can be sold to other breeders for house-sized prices. Earlier this year, Kazakh breeder Myktybayev posted a video of two Arashan rams being sold to an Uzbek breeder for a claimed total of $275,000. Some Kyrgyz commentators have compared the speculation frenzy over Arashans to Ponzi schemes, with debate breaking out online over reports of people taking out risky loans or selling cars or homes to buy breeding rams. In contrast to the fortunes paid for elite breeding animals, the price for an average adult Arashan is tied to the market price of mutton. Once slaughtered, an adult Arashan yields several hundred dollars' worth of mutton from its roughly 50–60 kilograms of meat at current market prices . An Arashan sheep being displayed during the September 19 fair near Bishkek. The Arashan sheep emerged from a breeding experiment that took place in the Kyrgyz city of Kant in the 1970s. "During the Soviet period there was an agricultural machine-testing station [in Kant] and its director at the time was a man named Zubkov," Satybekov told RFE/RL. "He brought breeding rams of the Hissar variety from Tajikistan and began crossing them with our indigenous local meat-and-fat sheep." There are currently around 48,000 Arashans in Kyrgyzstan, a fraction of the roughly 5.6 million total sheep population of the country. A corral of sheep at a collective farm in Soviet Kyrgyzstan in 1973. The record weight for an Arashan was set in June 2026 at 236 kilos (520 pounds), a fraction lighter than a Suffolk ram in the United States that tipped the scales at 247.2 kilos in 1991 to become the heaviest domestic sheep ever recorded. Amid a ban on sheep exports that sought to curb rising meat prices in Kyrgyzstan, an exemption was made for Arashans this summer. "Over the past two months, we've exported 215 Arashan sheep to Uzbekistan" since the ban was lifted for Arashans, Satybekov said. "There's also interest from Russia and farmers have visited us from Moldova and Georgia, as well. They're looking at how they can take animals back with them but for now we're working out how all of this can be done."
