https://cabar.asia/en/how-can-migrant-ch.body: © CABAR - Central Asian Bureau for Analytical Reporting Please make active links to the source, when using materials from this website На русском The publication “ Access to education for children of migrants in the Aktobe region of Kazakhstan: recommendations for the evidence-based decision making (policy brief) ” was prepared by Zhanna Sagyndykova with the support of the IWPR Representative Office in Central Asia and the regional analytical platform CABAR.asia. For citation and references to the material, please indicate: Zhanna Sagyndykova, Access to education for children of migrants in the Aktobe region of Kazakhstan: recommendations for the evidence-based decision making (policy brief) 2026, CABAR.asia. The primary objective of the study is to foster greater social integration and equal opportunities for all migrant children and, ultimately, to resolve the issue of school enrollment for all children of foreign nationals—regardless of their parents’ migration status—in accordance with the International Convention on the Rights of the Child, ratified by Kazakhstan in 1994. The publication notes that migrant children frequently face social isolation and discrimination within educational institutions. A lack of adequate social support and inclusive programs exacerbates challenges related to adaptation and academic success. The publication highlights that, following a project workshop titled “Planning an Advocacy Campaign Based on Existing Policy Briefs/White Papers,” a decision was made to adopt targeted engagement with government agencies as the primary advocacy method; this entails submitting direct inquiries to the relevant state bodies. The author proposes a series of specific recommendations for relevant agencies. In particular, Sagyndykova suggests amending the regulations governing education for the children of foreign nationals to eliminate legal conflicts and gaps, and proposes considering measures for their temporary registration and the granting of residence permits alongside their parents. It is also proposed that parents of foreign children be granted the right to choose their children’s school—a right they currently lack. Sagyndykova further argues that the term “labor migrants” needs to be clearly defined in legislation. Regional and district education departments are advised to ensure their specialists are promptly informed of any changes to bylaws concerning migrant children. Additionally, they are encouraged to develop measures to support migrant children during the adaptation process, as well as methods to monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of these measures.

© CABAR - Central Asian Bureau for Analytical Reporting Please make active links to the source, when using materials from this website На русском The publication “ Access to education for children of migrants in the Aktobe region of Kazakhstan: recommendations for the evidence-based decision making (white paper) ” was prepared by Zhanna Sagyndykova with the support of the IWPR Representative Office in Central Asia and the regional analytical platform CABAR.asia. For citation and references to the material, please indicate: Zhanna Sagyndykova, Access to education for children of migrants in the Aktobe region of Kazakhstan: recommendations for the evidence-based decision making (white paper) 2026, CABAR.asia. This study evaluates current policies regarding the education of migrant children in the Aktobe region of Kazakhstan and offers evidence-based recommendations to improve the situation in this area. Experts estimate that over 2 million migrants from neighboring Central Asian countries enter Kazakhstan annually. In December 2022, the Minister of Education of the Republic of Kazakhstan approved new regulations governing access to education for foreign nationals and stateless persons permanently residing in the country. The order specifies the categories of foreign nationals whose children are eligible to attend schools in Kazakhstan; however, these categories represent only a small fraction of the foreign nationals actually present in the country. Furthermore, the order contains contradictions, gaps, and inconsistencies that hinder its implementation. As a result, a large number of children of foreign nationals have been deprived of the right to school education. These include the children of irregular migrants temporarily present in the country without the right to legal employment, as well as the children of undocumented migrants, those with undetermined citizenship status, and others. The report notes that it is impossible to determine the exact number of foreign children who are ineligible to attend schools in Kazakhstan. Between December 2024 and October 2025, the “Daris-2016” Public Foundation conducted a comprehensive and detailed analysis of the situation, comprising two sequential stages: Desk research: December 2024 – March 2025; II. Data collection: February – October 2025. The analysis identified key barriers hindering access to education and educational integration for migrant children. These include gaps and contradictions in the legislative framework, a lack of awareness among migrants regarding their children’s right to education, a shortage of statistical data on key indicators, language barriers, and insufficient coordination among relevant agencies. The issues identified also result in the inadequate implementation of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration—agreements to which Kazakhstan is a party. As a result of this work, recommendations have been developed for government agencies, local self-government bodies, educational institutions, and migrant families; these recommendations aim to eliminate barriers preventing the educational integration of migrant children in the Aktobe region. Implementing these recommendations will, in particular, facilitate the development of more effective support strategies and programs, thereby creating conditions for the better adaptation of migrant children.

https://www.amnesty.org/fr/latest/news/2.body: « Les autorités algériennes doivent renoncer à tout projet visant à élargir le champ d’application de la peine de mort ou à reprendre les exécutions après plus de trois décennies d’interruption », a déclaré Amnesty International alors que le gouvernement examine des amendements au Code pénal qui étendraient l’usage de la peine de mort. Elle appelle le pouvoir algérien à instaurer immédiatement un moratoire officiel, à titre de premier pas sur la voie de l’abolition totale de la peine capitale. Elle l’engage aussi à adopter une approche axée sur les droits humains face aux récents incendies dévastateurs, notamment en menant des enquêtes efficaces sur tous les facteurs ayant conduit à des décès tragiques et en veillant à ce que les responsables rendent des comptes sans recourir à la peine de mort. Le 30 août, le président algérien Abdelmadjid Tebboune a enjoint au ministre de la Justice de réviser le Code pénal d’ici le 15 septembre afin de « réintroduire » la peine de mort pour les « auteurs et commanditaires » d’incendies volontaires. Il a insisté sur le fait que toute personne condamnée à mort serait exécutée dès qu’elle aurait épuisé ses voies de recours. Cette directive fait suite aux incendies meurtriers qui se sont déclarés entre le 26 et le 30 août, anéantissant des villages entiers dans la région de la Kabylie et d’autres parties du nord-est de l’Algérie. Le 6 septembre, le gouvernement a commencé à examiner le projet de révision du Code pénal et le président a indiqué que la peine de mort serait aussi instaurée pour les « ravisseurs et agresseurs d’enfants ». « Les ravages et les décès causés par ces incendies sont une terrible tragédie et doivent inciter les autorités algériennes à prendre des mesures immédiates axées à la fois sur la prévention et l’obligation de rendre des comptes. Toutefois, tirer un trait sur plus de 30 ans sans exécutions est une réponse rétrograde qui va à l’encontre du respect du droit à la vie, a déclaré Nadege Lahmar, chercheuse sur l’Algérie. « Cela piétine également les obligations internationales de l’Algérie en matière de droits humains, ainsi que son soutien constant aux résolutions de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies appelant à un moratoire sur les exécutions en vue d’abolir la peine de mort. » Amnesty International estime que la peine capitale constitue une violation du droit à la vie et qu’elle est le châtiment le plus cruel, inhumain et dégradant qui soit, qui n’a pas d’effet dissuasif spécifique sur la criminalité et perpétue un cycle de violences. En s’appuyant sur de précédents travaux de recherche sur les procès à caractère politique en Algérie, Amnesty International a passé en revue les déclarations publiques du gouvernement algérien ainsi que les articles parus dans les médias depuis le début des incendies, et analysé les dispositions légales applicables en cas d’incendies volontaires. Le 7 septembre, Amnesty International a fait part de ses préoccupations et de ses recommandations aux autorités algériennes. Au moment de la rédaction du présent communiqué, elle n’avait pas encore reçu de réponse. Les incendies ne doivent pas servir à justifier la répression Le gouvernement algérien n’a pas communiqué de chiffres complets quant au nombre de morts et de blessés causés par les incendies de forêt. Au 26 août, les chiffres officiels faisaient état de 12 morts et 54 hospitalisations , mais des sources fiables ont depuis rapporté un bilan nettement plus lourd , avec notamment plus de 70 morts dans une seule municipalité . En juillet, d’autres incendies avaient fait six morts , également dans le nord-est du pays. Alors que les autorités avaient établi un lien entre les feux de forêt de juillet et une vague de chaleur intense et avaient qualifié les incendies de risque majeur et de défi structurel aggravé par le changement climatique, au mois d’août, le président algérien a évoqué la piste criminelle , ayant pour objectif d’« affaiblir l’Algérie et de porter atteinte à son unité ». Entre le 26 juillet et le 10 septembre , les autorités algériennes ont annoncé le placement en détention de 20 personnes dans le cadre d’enquêtes pour incendie volontaire et « subversion » – un chef d’accusation lié au terrorisme passible de la peine de mort obligatoire. Elles ont affirmé qu’un sympathisant du Mouvement pour l’autodétermination de la Kabylie (MAK), un groupe politique d’opposition qualifié de « terroriste », en faisait partie. Elles ont déjà utilisé les feux de forêt pour justifier la répression et recourir à la peine de mort. À la suite des incendies survenus en août 2021 dans le nord-est de l’Algérie, qui avaient fait au moins 90 morts, elles ont accusé des groupes d’opposition politique, principalement le MAK, et intenté des poursuites en justice contre des dizaines de personnes pour des faits liés au terrorisme et d’autres infractions graves. En novembre 2022, un tribunal a déclaré coupables et condamné à mort 56 personnes à l’issue d’un procès collectif entaché de violations flagrantes du droit à un procès équitable et d’allégations de torture n’ayant pas fait l’objet d’enquêtes ; au moins 10 d’entre elles ont été condamnées à mort en raison de leurs affiliations politiques. La Cour suprême a par la suite ordonné la tenue d’un nouveau procès, qui a débuté le 1er mars 2026. Depuis 2021, les tribunaux ont invoqué des chefs d’accusation liés au terrorisme et motivés par des considérations politiques, passibles de la peine de mort, afin de poursuivre des militant·e·s pacifiques dans au moins deux autres affaires sans rapport avec les feux de forêt. Ce bilan rend d’autant plus inquiétant le projet d’élargir le champ d’application de la peine de mort. Il est nécessaire d’apporter une réponse axée sur les droits humains Alors que l’Algérie se retrouve confrontée à des feux de forêt de plus en plus fréquents et intenses dans un contexte d’accélération du réchauffement dû au changement climatique, il importe de concentrer les efforts sur la protection des vies humaines, le renforcement de la prévention et des interventions d’urgence, notamment en s’attaquant aux causes profondes des catastrophes exacerbées par le climat, la tenue d’enquêtes crédibles et l’obligation de rendre des comptes. « Cette obligation concernant les terribles pertes en vies humaines causées par les feux de forêt ne saurait se limiter à poursuivre les auteurs présumés d’incendies volontaires. Les autorités doivent mener des enquêtes approfondies, indépendantes, impartiales et transparentes sur tous les facteurs ayant provoqué ou contribué aux incendies et aux décès, y compris les éventuelles défaillances des responsables publics et les lacunes en matière de prévention, de préparation et d’intervention d’urgence, a déclaré Nadege Lahmar. « Il faut rendre les conclusions publiques et, lorsqu’il existe des preuves suffisantes de responsabilité pénale, engager des poursuites dans le cadre de procédures équitables excluant le recours à la peine de mort. Enfin, les victimes et les familles ont le droit de recevoir en temps utile des informations accessibles et précises au sujet des personnes disparues ou décédées. » Contexte En vertu de la législation algérienne en vigueur, l’incendie volontaire est passible de peines allant de trois ans à la réclusion à perpétuité, voire de la peine de mort s’il entraîne la mort d’autrui. Bien que l’Algérie n’ait procédé à aucune exécution depuis 1993, les tribunaux continuent de prononcer des condamnations à mort, le plus souvent pour meurtre . En juillet 2025, le champ d’application de la peine de mort avait déjà été élargi pour y inclure plusieurs infractions liées au trafic de stupéfiants . L’Algérie est partie au Pacte international relatif aux droits civils et politiques (PIDCP), qui réserve le recours à la peine de mort aux « crimes les plus graves », étant entendu qu’il s’agit d’infractions impliquant un homicide volontaire, et qui fixe comme objectif son abolition dans les pays qui maintiennent encore c

En réaction à la condamnation des militant·e·s ayant organisé des veillées en commémoration de Tiananmen à Hong Kong, Sarah Brooks, directrice régionale adjointe à Amnesty International, a déclaré : « Pendant la majeure partie des 30 années au cours desquelles les habitant·e·s de Hong Kong ont commémoré la répression de Tiananmen en organisant chaque année une veillée à la lueur des bougies, il aurait été impensable que les organisateurs de cet événement puissent être incarcérés pour leur militantisme pacifique. La condamnation prononcée aujourd’hui illustre à quel point Hong Kong a changé au nom de la » sécurité nationale « . « Ces condamnations constituent une triple tragédie : pour les militant·e·s injustement sanctionnés, pour les survivants et les victimes de la répression de Tiananmen, et pour les générations de Hongkongais·e·s privés de tout espace pour discuter de l’un des événements les plus marquants de l’histoire contemporaine de la Chine. « La persécution des militant·e·s de Tiananmen met en évidence la peur profonde des voix dissidentes qui caractérise le régime fondé sur la » sécurité nationale » de Hong Kong. Cependant, on ne renforce pas la sécurité nationale en emprisonnant des personnes qui rendent un hommage pacifique à leurs morts. « Les autorités doivent penser que le fait de sanctionner des personnalités influentes aura un effet dissuasif sur la population, mais l’histoire démontre que les revendications en faveur de la vérité et de l’obligation de rendre des comptes ne s’évaporent pas simplement parce qu’elles sont érigées en infractions. « La condamnation prononcée aujourd’hui est une insulte à la mémoire des victimes et un affront à l’histoire. Les militant·e·s de l’Alliance de Hong Kong n’ont commis aucun crime reconnu par le droit international et doivent être libérés immédiatement et sans condition. Il importe de protéger leur droit de faire appel de ces peines de prison iniques. » Contexte Le 11 septembre 2026, la Haute Cour de Hong Kong a condamné l’avocate Chow Hang-tung à sept ans et trois mois de prison et son collègue militant de Tiananmen, Lee Cheuk-yan, à sept ans de prison pour « incitation à la subversion du pouvoir de l’État », en vertu de la Loi sur la sécurité nationale de la ville. Albert Ho Chun-yan, qui avait auparavant plaidé coupable du même chef d’accusation, a été condamné à cinq ans et deux mois de prison. Chow Hang-tung et Lee Cheuk-yan comptaient parmi les sept membres de l’Alliance de Hong Kong pour le soutien des mouvements démocratiques patriotiques en Chine (Alliance de Hong Kong) inculpés en septembre 2021 de différentes infractions en vertu de la loi imposée par Pékin. Tous deux se trouvent en détention provisoire depuis lors, leur demande de libération sous caution ayant été rejetée à plusieurs reprises. Amnesty International les a adoptés comme prisonniers d’opinion. Amnesty International a fait part à plusieurs reprises de son inquiétude quant au fait que la loi sur la sécurité nationale, promulguée en juin 2020, sert à cibler des organisations de la société civile, des journalistes, des militant·e·s politiques, des universitaires et d’autres, pour des actions qui sont pleinement protégées par le droit international relatif aux droits humains. Les veillées de Tiananmen commémoraient les événements du 4 juin 1989, lorsque des soldats chinois ont ouvert le feu sur des étudiant·e·s et des travailleurs·euses qui manifestaient pacifiquement en faveur de réformes politiques sur la place Tiananmen et alentour, à Pékin. Des centaines, voire des milliers de personnes ont été tuées. Des dizaines de milliers d’autres ont été arrêtées dans toute la Chine dans le cadre de la répression qui a déferlé. Au cours des 37 années qui ont suivi, toute discussion concernant cet événement a fait l’objet d’une censure sévère en Chine, et les autorités l’ont de fait effacé de leur version de l’histoire. Dès le début, il a été interdit de commémorer la répression de Tiananmen en Chine continentale. Mais à Hong Kong, des foules rassemblant plusieurs centaines de milliers de personnes se retrouvaient chaque année au Victoria Park, situé en centre-ville, pour rendre un hommage pacifique aux victimes. Les participant·e·s demandaient régulièrement aux autorités chinoises de révéler la vérité sur ce qui s’était passé et d’assumer la responsabilité de ces atrocités ; pendant 30 ans, le gouvernement local n’est pas intervenu et ne s’y est pas opposé. La dernière grande veillée organisée par l’Alliance de Hong Kong a eu lieu en 2019. Elle a ensuite été interdite en 2020 et 2021, soi-disant en raison de la pandémie de Covid-19. Depuis, la loi sur la sécurité nationale érige en infraction, dans la pratique, les manifestations pacifiques dans la ville, y compris les commémorations de Tiananmen.

https://rsf.org/fr/quatre-ans-apr%C3%A8s.body: Quatre ans après le mouvement “Femme, vie, liberté” en Iran, le régime prépare une nouvelle offensive contre la presse Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel La très lourde peine de 15 ans de prison infligée à la journaliste indépendante Yalda Moaiery, en août dernier, marque un nouvel épisode de l'escalade dans l’offensive contre la liberté de la presse en Iran. Quatre ans après le mouvement “Femme, vie, liberté” et la terrible répression du journalisme qui s’ensuivit, le régime est en passe d’approuver une nouvelle loi liberticide. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) appelle le Conseil des gardiens de la constitution à abandonner ce texte qui s’attaque tant aux sources qu’aux journalistes en Iran, où au moins 19 professionnels de l’information sont actuellement détenus. Yalda Moaiery n'a jamais reçu sa convocation au tribunal. Les autorités l'avaient envoyée en août par SMS à un numéro qu'elles avaient elles-mêmes bloqué, selon la journaliste. Rien de surprenant en Iran, pays classé 177e sur 180 dans le Classement mondial de la liberté de la presse de RSF. Depuis décembre, régulièrement, le régime coupe l’accès à Internet, bloque les cartes SIM des journalistes et leur interdit de communiquer avec des médias à l’étranger sous peine d'être accusés d'espionnage. C’est ainsi que Yalda Moaiery, photojournaliste indépendante qui couvre l’Iran et la région depuis 20 ans pour plusieurs médias internationaux – dont le quotidien français Le Monde, le magazine américain Time , et le quotidien espagnol El Pais – s’est trouvée, ce 8 août, condamnée par contumace à 15 ans de prison pour avoir photographié l’offensive américano-israélienne en début d’année. “J'ai pu me défendre lors d’une nouvelle audience au tribunal [le 1er septembre], mais le jury ne semblait pas m'écouter,” confie-t-elle à RSF depuis l’Iran, où le pouvoir judiciaire relève de l'autorité du Guide suprême. “La République islamique ne peut tolérer des journalistes qui travaillent librement” , résume-t-elle. Accusée d’avoir “collaboré avec des médias étrangers dans le but de renforcer le régime sioniste et les États-Unis”, la journaliste a vu sa peine confirmée le 1er septembre et attend son procès en appel. Découvrez le témoignage de Yalda Moaiery Visionnez la vidéo Une nouvelle loi en toile de fond Cette lourde peine de 15 ans de prison s’inscrit dans une repression accrue du journalisme, qui s'intensifie depuis le déclenchement du mouvement “Femme, vie, liberté” en 2022. Et cette répression pourrait encore s’intensifier avec une loi draconienne, actuellement en chantier. “Participer à des entretiens avec des médias ou des professionnels des médias qualifiés d'hostiles par le ministère du Renseignement [...] est interdit” , peut-on lire, par exemple, dans l’article 22 de ce “plan de lutte contre l'influence étrangère”. Ce projet de loi vient en fait donner un vernis légal à des restrictions qui avaient déjà cours qui se sont généralisées depuis la guerre de mars 2026 entre l’Iran et la coalition israélo-américaine : en effet, ces communications étaient déjà criminalisées dans la pratique. Il vient également élargir la définition de l'“espionnage”, et ainsi permettre d’incriminer sans difficulté les journalistes, ainsi que leurs sources. Les dispositions de cette nouvelle loi, approuvée par le Parlement le 16 août dernier, doivent encore être débattues par le Conseil des gardiens de la constitution avant d’entrer en vigueur. Aucune date n'a été fixée pour cette ultime décision. “La peine de prison scandaleuse infligée à Yalda Moaiery, qui doit être immédiatement annulée, est une continuation d’une repression d’État qui ne fait que s’intensifier depuis le déclenchement du mouvement Femme, vie, liberté en 2022, avec la détention de plus de 100 journalistes qui le couvraient, parmi lesquels 19 croupissent encore en prison. Mais la peine inédite de Yalda Moaery, si elle est confirmée en appel, ne sera qu'un avant-goût de ce qui attend les journalistes et leur sources une fois la nouvelle loi adoptée. Cette nouvelle législation visant à faciliter les arrestations et renforcer l’autocensure, ne sert qu’à légitimer la répression illégale d’une dictature, et doit impérativement être rejetée. Les journalistes doivent être libérés, et la République islamique doit cesser d’instrumentaliser la sécurité nationale pour étouffer son peuple et ses journalistes.” Jonathan Dagher Responsable du bureau Moyen-Orient de RSF Une loi qui criminalise toute collaboration avec des médias étrangers Ce nouveau projet de loi dépasse les textes législatifs préexistants qui sanctionnaient la propagande contre l'État ou la collaboration avec un État hostile, en criminalisant explicitement le fait de s'exprimer dans des médias “liés aux États-Unis ou à Israël”. Les ressortissants iraniens seraient également dans l'obligation de demander une autorisation pour répondre à toute demande d'entretien d'un média étranger, même lorsque celui-ci n’est pas lié à l’un de ces deux pays ennemis de la République islamique. “Au lieu de définir précisément l’espionnage, [la loi] recourt à des notions extrêmement larges telles que la ‘collaboration’” , explique l’avocat iranien Mousa Barzin, exilé en Turquie. “Ce ne sont pas seulement les journalistes qui sont concernés : tout employé, médecin, infirmier, avocat ou autre citoyen susceptible de constituer une source d’information risque, par crainte de sanctions, de garder le silence.” Dix-neuf journalistes détenus, et les condamnations continuent Depuis la répression d’ampleur des journalistes qui couvraient le mouvement “Femme, vie, liberté” en 2022, plus de 100 professionnels des médias ont été détenus en raison de leur travail, dont 19 sont encore en prison. D’autres font face à des procédures judiciaires inextricables. Le journaliste Mehdi Mahmoudian, arrêté le 31 janvier a été condamné, le 13 août, à huit mois de prison pour "propagande contre le régime" pour avoir simplement couvert les circonstances de la guerre sur ses réseaux sociaux. Son confrère, le blogueur Soheil Arabi , lauréat 2017 du prix RSF dans la catégorie "journaliste-citoyen", a lui été condamné, trois jours plus tard, à cinq ans de prison pour "association et collusion en vue de commettre un crime contre la sécurité nationale". D’autres condamnés sont en liberté conditionnelle mais risquent à tout moment de retrouver leur geôle. Parmi ceux-là, Narges Mohammadi, la journaliste iranienne, écrivaine et lauréate du prix Nobel de la paix en 2023, actuellement en liberté pour raison médicale, mais régulièrement harcelée par les autorités et menacée d'emprisonnement. Les mesures de répression en Iran s’inscrivent dans une tendance mondiale d’instrumentaliser la sécurité nationale pour réprimer la liberté de la presse et resserrer l’étau sur le droit à l’information, comme le révèle un rapport de RSF . Depuis le début de la guerre en Iran en Mars 2026, et ses répercussions dans le Golfe, plusieurs régimes de la zone ont instauré des mesures liberticides pour empêcher la couverture du conflit. https://rsf.org/fr/b%C3%A9larus-quatre-p.body: Bélarus : quatre professionnels des médias libérés et expulsés, RSF dénonce le “carrousel répressif” de Minsk RSF Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Dzmitry Navajylau, Andreï Aliaksandrau, Kiryl Pazniak et Lioudmila Tchekina ont été libérés ce 16 septembre aux côtés d’autres prisonniers politiques au Bélarus, avant d’être immédiatement conduits en Lituanie. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) se réjouit de les voir enfin libres, mais dénonce leur expulsion forcée et appelle les autorités biélorusses à relâcher immédiatement et sans condition tous les journalistes encore détenus dans le pays. Une liberté retrouvée, mais au prix de l’exil. Quatre professionnels des médias figurent parmi les 25 prisonniers politiques libérés par les autorités biélorusses ce 16 septembre et conduits en Lituanie : Lioudmila Tchekina, Dzmitry Navajylau , Andreï Aliaksandrau et Kiryl Pazniak . En échange de leur libération, les États-Unis ont commencé à lever certaines sanctions visant le régime biélorusse, notamment celles frappant des entreprises du secteur de la potasse et la compagnie aérienne nationale Belavia. “Nous nous réjouissons de voir Dzmitry Navajylau, Andreï Aliaksandrau, Lioudmila Tchekina et Kiryl Pazniak enfin libres. Mais leur libération ne saurait faire oublier qu’ils n’auraient jamais dû être emprisonnés. Les contraindre à quitter immédiatement leur pays ajoute une nouvelle violence à des années de répression. Le cas de Dzmitry Navajylau, à qui il ne restait que deux mois de peine à purger, illustre particulièrement la brutalité de cette pratique. Ce carrousel répressif, où des prisonniers politiques sont relâchés tandis que d’autres sont arrêtés et condamnés, doit cesser. Les journalistes ne doivent être ni emprisonnés pour leur travail, ni bannis de leur propre pays. RSF appelle les autorités biélorusses à relâcher immédiatement et sans condition tous les professionnels des médias encore détenus. Jeanne Cavelier Responsable du bureau Europe de l’Est et Asie centrale de RSF Cette nouvelle vague de libérations intervient après plusieurs opérations similaires ces derniers mois. En mars 2026, six professionnels des médias avaient été graciés lors de la libération de près de 250 prisonniers politiques, négociée entre les États-Unis et Alexandre Loukachenko. Le journaliste polono-biélorusse Andrzej Poczobut avait ensuite retrouvé la liberté le 28 avril, après plus de cinq années de détention arbitraire, dans le cadre d'un échange de prisonniers. Des années derrière les barreaux Dzmitry Navazhylau , ancien directeur de l’agence de presse indépendante BelaPAN , était détenu depuis le 18 août 2021. Le 6 octobre 2022, il avait été condamné à six ans de prison pour “évasion fiscale” et “création d’une formation extrémiste ou participation à celle-ci”. Déjà gracié lors de la précédente vague de remises en liberté, il n’avait plus que deux mois de peine à purger lorsqu’il a finalement quitté sa prison ce 16 septembre, avant d’être immédiatement conduit en Lituanie. Andreï Aliaksandrau , ancien directeur adjoint de BelaPAN , journaliste et défenseur de la liberté de la presse au parcours international, a notamment travaillé pour Index on Censorship et ARTICLE 19. Arrêté le 12 janvier 2021 avec son épouse, Irina Zlobina, il avait été condamné le 6 octobre 2022 à 14 ans de prison pour “haute trahison”, “participation à un groupe extrémiste”, “troubles à l’ordre public” et “évasion fiscale”. Condamnée à neuf ans de prison dans la même affaire, Irina Zlobina a elle aussi été libérée ce 16 septembre. Lioudmila Tchekina , directrice de TUT.by , autrefois le média en ligne le plus populaire du pays et fermé par les autorités en 2021 , avait été arrêtée le 18 mai 2021 et condamnée à 12 ans de prison aux côtés de sa rédactrice en chef Maryna Zolatava , notamment pour “évasion fiscale”, “organisation d’incitation à la haine sociale” et “diffusion de contenus appelant à des actions portant atteinte à la sécurité nationale”. Détenue pendant plus de cinq ans, elle avait refusé de signer une lettre reconnaissant sa culpabilité. Kiryl Pazniak , journaliste et fondateur de Platforma 375 , média déclaré “formation extrémiste” en septembre 2025, avait été condamné le 26 juin 2026 à trois ans et demi de prison pour “création d’une formation extrémiste ou participation à celle-ci” et “discrédit de la République du Bélarus”. Souffrant de graves complications après une pneumonie et la COVID-19 contractées en détention, il avait dû être hospitalisé et placé sous assistance respiratoire. Sa fille, Yanina Pazniak, elle-même condamnée notamment pour avoir créé le compte TikTok du média, a également été libérée. Une répression qui se poursuit Ces remises en liberté successives témoignent aussi de l’utilisation des prisonniers politiques comme monnaie d’échange dans les négociations avec les puissances occidentales, notamment en contrepartie d’allègements de sanctions. Elles ne marquent en rien la fin de l’offensive contre la presse indépendante : à cette heure, 17 professionnels des médias sont encore détenus au Bélarus. Depuis la répression des manifestations post-électorales de 2020, les autorités biélorusses ont multiplié les poursuites contre les journalistes et les médias indépendants, dont la plupart ont été contraints à l’exil. En mars dernier, alors que plusieurs journalistes venaient d'être graciés, RSF constatait simultanément de nouvelles condamnations de professionnels des médias à de lourdes peines de prison, notamment jusqu'à 14 ans de détention . https://www.rferl.org/a/us-charges-five-.body: Russia US Charges 5 In Russian Intelligence Sabotage And Assassination Plot By Mike Eckel September 16, 2026 11:15 CET Updated September 16, 2026 13:41 CET US Charges 5 In Russian Intelligence Sabotage And Assassination Plot Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian intelligence agencies oversaw a series of surveillance and assassination plots targeting dissidents in the United States and Europe, US authorities charged, adding to a growing number of warnings about Russian spy operations in the West. The allegations, detailed in a new federal indictment, were also the latest warning from Western officials detailing how Russia increasingly uses people not trained as professional spies --- sometimes unwittingly -- to carry out operations. Among the five people charged in the indictment unveiled late on September 15: a father and son linked to Russia's Federal Security Service: Kirill Khrameyev, identified as a colonel in the agency, known as the FSB; his father, Yury, identified as a retired FSB officer. Three others -- two Cuban men named Oemis Durruthy and Yaidel Suarez and a Venezuelan man Angel Castro -- were also charged. Durruthy lives in Russia, the US Justice Department said in a statement . The whereabouts of the two others are unclear. According to the indictment, as recently as this summer, Castro, who had been living in Brooklyn, New York, was hired to surveil a prominent Russian dissident who was living in Washington, D.C. The Russian dissident is not identified in the court filings. The person was sent to two addresses and given “explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance,” authorities said. In exchange, the person was promised $1,000 and $1,500 to carry out the surveillance. The person then allegedly sent photographs to one of the FSB officers, who then later offered $40,000 to the person to “eliminate” or “disappear” the dissident. After the person declined the offer, the FSB officers allegedly sought out others in the United States to carry out the murder plot. SEE ALSO: 'You Wanted Turmoil. You Got It': How FSB Officers Chatted, And Plotted, To Sow Discord In The U.S. In another incident detailed in the indictment, an American man living in Lithuania traveled to Estonia, to the border with Russia on June 25, 2025. There, he met Khrameyev who allegedly offered to pay the man an unspecified amount to return to Vilnius and take photographs of an address where a “bad guy” who was “telling lies about Russia" lived. The person was paid $200 for the surveillance. The person was then put in touch with Khrameyev’s father, Yury, who allegedly offered him $25,000 to kill the person because he was "spreading dirt about my country" and "telling the media and the common people that the Russians are the aggressors." Khrameyev also explained how the killing could take place, including "throwing a bottle of gasoline" or "sticking a knife" in the person," according to the court filing. After the person declined, Yury Khrameyev allegedly proposed he could set fire to a warehouse or electrical substation for an unspecified amount of money. Khrameyev allegedly wrote to the man, saying he was offering "serious money for serious work," and he was interested in targeting pro-Ukrainian countries, according to the indictment. The group was also accused of a plot to set fire to buses in the Czech Republic. Durruthy, US authorities said, enlisted a Colombian man, who allegedly tried to burn public buses in the capital, Prague. After the man's arrest, the Czech prime minister said the plot was "very likely" organized by Russian authorities. The FSB had no immediate comment on the charges. Neither Yury nor Kirill Khrameyev could be reached for comment either. Photographs posted by Kirill Khrameyev to the Russian social media platform VK show him posing at a St. Petersburg academy graduation ceremony, alongside his father. Kirill Khrameyev (left) and his father, FSB officer Yury Khrameyev, are shown in a 2016 social media post, posing at graduation ceremony for a St. Petersburg military academy. The indictment includes extensive quoted material taken from chat messages, as well as photographs, that were exchanged between the Khrameyevs and their contacts. It does not specify how the material was gathered, but in past years, US authorities have used search warrants to access cloud-based storage services -- for example Apple's iCloud, or Google Drive -- to obtain backed-up files, including things like WhatsApp chat logs. Other plots have been uncovered by authorities accessing Google Translate files stored online, according to the investigative website The Insider . https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-sanctions.body: News Russia Sanctions Bill Clears Another Hurdle, Heads Toward Final Vote In US Congress By Alex Raufoglu September 16, 2026 10:10 CET Russia Sanctions Bill Clears Another Hurdle, Heads Toward Final Vote In US Congress Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Republican Representative Michael McCaul of Texas, who is managing the legislation on the House floor. (file photo) WASHINGTON -- A sweeping Russia sanctions bill championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham cleared a key procedural hurdle in the US House of Representatives on September 15, setting up a final vote on legislation that supporters say would increase pressure on Moscow and strengthen US support for Ukraine. The House voted 214-211 to approve a rule allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, with two Democrats joining Republicans voting in favor. Many Democrats oppose the bill because it would give President Donald Trump additional power to impose tariffs. The vote cleared the way for the House to consider the version approved by the Senate with strong bipartisan support in August, and a final vote in the 435-seat chamber is expected on September 16. If it approves the Senate text without changes, the bill would go to Trump. "We're going to get done tomorrow," Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska told RFE/RL, expressing confidence that the House would pass the bill. "At least that's the least we could do. We've got to do more." The legislation would impose sanctions on Russian officials and military figures, foreign suppliers supporting Russia's defense sector, and networks helping Moscow evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia's so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers, restrict new US investment in Russia and exports that could support the Russian military, and authorize sanctions against people responsible for abducting Ukrainian children. The measure also extends sanctions on Iran. SEE ALSO: US House Set To Take Up Russia Sanctions Bill Amid Fight Over Trump Tariff Powers In addition, it would allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries purchasing Russian energy or helping Moscow evade sanctions. The tariff provisions have drawn opposition from mostly Democratic lawmakers concerned about granting additional trade authority to Trump and about potential effects on US fuel prices. The Senate rejected an effort to remove the provisions before passing the legislation. 'Scorching Sanctions' Republican Representative Michael McCaul of Texas, who is managing the legislation on the House floor, portrayed its expected passage as part of Graham's legacy. "One of the proudest accomplishments I think I've had is the bill we're going to pass tomorrow that Lindsey Graham said, in his words, if I'm not mistaken, the biggest legislative accomplishment of his career," McCaul said at an event at Ukraine House in Washington marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's restored independence. Graham, a South Carolina Republican and prominent supporter of Ukraine, died in July. Late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham (right) and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal speak to reporters while on a visit to Kyiv earlier this year. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who worked with Graham on the legislation, said at the same event that the measure would impose "scorching sanctions" intended to "throttle Putin's war machine." Divisions over the tariff provisions have complicated the bill's path through the House. Republican Representative Tim Burchett of Tennessee said he had received assurances that Republican leaders would consider measures aimed at reducing fuel costs. 'A Symbolic Win For Ukraine' Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and a supporter of the legislation, has urged the House to approve it, saying it would target financial resources sustaining Russia's war and increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin to negotiate. The sanctions push comes as Ukraine continues to seek US military and economic support more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. Andrew D'Anieri, associate director of the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center, told RFE/RL that enactment of the bill would be "a symbolic win for Ukraine," but said Kyiv also needed continued military assistance, particularly air defenses. At the Ukraine House event, US Under Secretary of the Treasury for International Affairs Jonathan Greenstein said Washington remained committed to "achieving a negotiated settlement and a durable peace" while supporting an "independent and prosperous future for Ukraine." Greenstein said the United States had disbursed $7.5 billion to Ukraine in 2026 and expected to provide nearly $300 million more in the coming months. https://www.rferl.org/a/centcom-hormuz-h.body: Iran CENTCOM Says Hormuz 'Remains Open' As Houthi-Saudi Fighting Threatens Another Key Waterway By RFE/RL September 16, 2026 18:42 CET CENTCOM Says Hormuz 'Remains Open' As Houthi-Saudi Fighting Threatens Another Key Waterway Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. (file photo) The US military says traffic in the Strait of Hormuz continues to gain momentum amid concerns that escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen threatens another vital artery for global oil supplies in the region. CENTCOM said in a statement to RFE/RL on September 16 that the strait "remains open for transit." A key artery for global energy supplies, the strategic waterway has been a focal point in the war between the United States and Iran. "Traffic is flowing and momentum is building despite Iranian attempts to intimidate and harm innocent civilian crews," the statement said. SEE ALSO: What Houthi Gains In Yemen Mean For The Iran War "In recent months, thousands of commercial ships and nearly one billion barrels of oil have transited through the strait. Iran clearly does not control it. The international waterway remains open for transit," it added. Commercial traffic through Hormuz has plunged since the Iran war began in February. Tehran has sought to assert control over navigation through the strait and has attacked commercial vessels, while the United States is enforcing a naval blockade aimed at preventing ships from serving Iranian ports and has also attacked Iran-linked vessels. Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz handled about one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, making it one of the world's most important energy chokepoints. Around 125 large commercial vessels a day typically passed through the waterway before the conflict. Meanwhile, Houthi rebels in Yemen have captured ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea in recent days, threatening the flow of oil through another main shipping artery in the Middle East. Saudi Arabian warplanes pounded Yemen on September 16 while Houthi fighters launched drones and missiles at Saudi cities as the clashes continue to escalate. The Houthis have fired repeatedly into Saudi Arabia over the past week. An attack attributed to the Iran-aligned fighters in Iraq last week knocked out Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, the main route it has used to divert oil exports with the Strait of Hormuz blocked. https://www.rferl.org/a/islam-hijab-ban-.body: Features Central Asia's Hijab Debate Flares Up As Schools Reopen By Farangis Najibullah September 16, 2026 09:44 CET Central Asia's Hijab Debate Flares Up As Schools Reopen Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Kyrgyz women hijab look on as they take part in celebrations for World Hijab Day in Bishkek. Kyrgyzstan is the only Central Asian country that has not officially banned the hijab, although the issue is a matter of debate there. (file photo) Listen to this article 5 min This audio is automated Learn more As a practicing Muslim, Gulbarg wears the hijab, or Islamic head scarf, and prays five times a day. But in Tajikistan, a Muslim-majority country where a staunchly secular government has been in power for decades, she is seen as "some kind of threat," said Gulbarg, whose name has been changed for security reasons. "On the first day of university, a professor politely reminded me that the hijab is banned at schools," Gulbarg, a student at Khujand State University in northern Tajikistan, told RFE/RL. "She said, 'Personally, I don't have anything against your hijab, but the law is the law.'" The hijab has long been a hot topic in Muslim-majority Central Asia, where governments have sought to restrict independent Islamic activity and regulate religious expression. That includes the hijab. Rules over Islamic head coverings vary across the region, but they are banned in public schools and government offices in Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan. That debate has flared up again as millions of students flocked back to school and university for the start of the new academic year this month. SEE ALSO: Kyrgyzstan Bans Islamic Niqab As Critics Warn It Could Alienate Some Women Matter Of National Security In Kazakhstan, Education Minister Zhuldyz Suleimenova warned that private schools allowing girls to wear the hijab "could be deprived of their licenses." The warning has created a dilemma for some schools in Kazakhstan. A teacher working at a public school in the southern Kazakh city of Shymkent said several girls in her class have refused to remove their head scarves. "The principal and deputy principal don't know on what grounds they can remove the girls from school," the teacher, speaking on condition of anonymity because she was not authorized to speak to the media, told RFE/RL's Kazakh Service. "The school even conducted an unscheduled writing test, apparently hoping that poor grades could provide a reason to expel them." But all four girls passed the test, the teacher said. In 2016, Kazakhstan's Education Ministry issued a decree on student uniforms that prohibited the wearing of religious symbols at school, including the hijab. Since then, the issue has pitted supporters of secular education against those who say Muslim girls should be allowed to wear the head scarf. Kazakh officials have portrayed the hijab issue as a matter of national security and the protection of the country's secular political system. Central Asia has grappled with Islamic extremism in recent years. But critics say the authorities have severely restricted any signs of Islam without addressing the causes of radicalization. Female students wear school uniforms at a school in Shymkent, Kazakhstan. 'Deep-Seated Fear Of Islam' Experts say the hijab debate reflects a broader struggle over how much space secular governments are willing to give religious expression. Davide Cancarini, a Milan-based researcher focusing on Central Asia, said the hijab is "the most visible element" of the debate. He said governments have promoted an official, moderate form of Islam while wary of the religion as an independent social and cultural force. "The deep-seated fear of Islam has led governments to suppress any form of religious practices that fall outside state control," Cancarini told RFE/RL. Ahmet Furkan Ozyakar, an expert on regional politics at Atatürk University in Turkey, said Islam is an important part of Kazakhstan's history and national identity, but religious activity remains closely regulated. "The hijab is particularly sensitive because it makes religious identity visible in an institution that the state explicitly defines as secular," Ozyakar said. He said governments in Central Asia do not necessarily see greater religiosity itself as a threat. "Their concern is often with religious expression or organizations outside state-regulated structures, particularly when they could become a source of independent social or political mobilization," Ozyakar told RFE/RL. SEE ALSO: Tajikistan Expands Crackdown On Head Scarves, Beards In New Push For 'National Culture' That fear is particularly visible in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, where police have carried out raids targeting women wearing the hijab and men with long beards . Both governments have justified their restrictions on Islamic clothing by claiming they are protecting secularism and national security. Tajikistan and Turkmenistan have also promoted traditional national clothing as an alternative to what the authorities regard as foreign forms of dress. Kyrgyzstan is the only Central Asian country that has not officially banned the hijab, although the issue has also generated debate there. RFE/RL's Kazakh Service contributed to this report. https://www.rferl.org/a/iran-cinema-woma.body: Iran Women, Life, Freedom Leaves Its Mark On A New Wave Of Iranian Cinema By Mehdi Tahbaz September 17, 2026 07:42 CET Women, Life, Freedom Leaves Its Mark On A New Wave Of Iranian Cinema Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Iranian director Ali Asgari and Iranian actress Sadaf Asgari attend the red carpet event for the screening of A Little Light, presented in competition at the 83rd International Venice Film Festival, on September 11. Four years after the death of Mahsa Amini sparked Iran's largest protest movement in decades, the impact of Women, Life, Freedom is in Iranian society. One of the movement's most lasting effects has been on the way Iranian filmmakers portray women. Characters who once had to navigate the restrictions imposed by Iran's censorship system are increasingly being presented as women who simply refuse to accept them. In Jafar Panahi's film It Was Just An Accident, one of the central female characters is unveiled, resolute, and pragmatic, forcing those around her to confront uncomfortable truths. Panahi has described the character as reflecting the women who took control of their own destinies during the Women, Life, Freedom protests. SEE ALSO: Dissident Iranian Filmmaker Panahi Wins At Cannes, Vows To Return To Tehran September 16 marks the fourth anniversary of Amini's death. Twenty-two years old at the time, Amini was held by the so-called morality police in Tehran for an alleged violation of the mandatory hijab law. After three days of detention, she died from what authorities said was heart failure. Eyewitnesses, including some women who were detained with Amini, however, said she was severely beaten by police. Her family said she was healthy before the arrest and blame police brutality for her death. The once-feared patrols that policed women's clothing head-to-toe have largely vanished from everyday street life since the mass protests of 2022. The compulsory hijab rules are still there, but their enforcement has visibly eased across Iran's major cities, previously battlegrounds for women fighting for their freedom. But the shift is not limited to the hijab. In Soheil Beiraghi's Bidad (Outcry), made in Iran without official authorization, the central conflict revolves around another prohibition imposed on women: singing in public. But the film's concern is ultimately larger than singing. The voice becomes a question of who is allowed to be seen and heard in public and who is expected to remain silent. When Seti, the film's protagonist, sings without waiting for permission, her act becomes a form of civil disobedience. The street, much as it did during the 2022 protests, becomes more than an ordinary public space; it transforms into a place for making demands and resisting restrictions. Embed share Defiant Iranian Film Spotlights Crackdown On Female Singers by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:37 0:00 A growing group of Iranian filmmakers have gone further, producing films outside the rules imposed by the Culture Ministry and without the official permits traditionally required to make and release a movie in Iran. They include Navid Mihandoust's The Cafe, Karim Lakzadeh's Dark Matter, Mehrnoush Aliya's A Thousand and One Frames, Sahand Kabiri's The Group, Mohammad Shirvani's Cesarean Weekend, Abbas Nezamdoost's Dual, and Ali Asgari's A Little Light, among others. The significance of these films lies not only in what they depict, but in how they are made. For decades, Iranian filmmakers learned to work within or around an elaborate censorship system. Social realities could be addressed, but they first had to be reshaped to fit what the authorities would permit. The filmmaker's task was often to find a way to tell the truth after passing it through the filter of censorship. The post-2022 films represent a different approach, and that is simply removing the filter. That decision has come at a cost. Legal cases have been opened against most of the above-named filmmakers and their crews, with some receiving prison sentences and fines. Their offense, in effect, has been to change cinema's relationship with the realities unfolding around them. The phenomenon did not begin with the Women, Life, Freedom movement. Iranian cinema has a long history of confronting censorship, while women filmmakers and actresses have spent decades pushing against restrictions on their representation and their bodies. Embed share Four Years After Mahsa Amini's Death, Iranian Women Defy Hijab Law by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:06 0:00 Direct link 240p | 4.2MB 360p | 5.7MB 480p | 8.2MB 720p | 13.2MB 1080p | 21.3MB But the September 2022 unrest undeniably accelerated a break with the status quo. Instead of asking how far they can push the boundaries of officially permitted cinema, an increasing number of filmmakers are asking what happens if they abandon those boundaries altogether. That has produced a parallel Iranian cinema, one that can be made without official permission, in which actresses can appear unveiled and women can sing, speak, and move through public spaces without the constraints imposed by the state. Iran's authorities can still control which films receive official permits and which can be shown in domestic cinemas. What has become harder to control, however, is the act of making the films themselves. And in the years since the 2022 protests, that may be the most consequential change of all. Iranian filmmakers are increasingly refusing to make reality pass through the state's filter before putting it on screen. https://www.rferl.org/a/us-congress-swee.body: News US Congress Passes Sweeping Russia Sanctions Bill, Sends It To Trump By Alex Raufoglu September 17, 2026 07:18 CET US Congress Passes Sweeping Russia Sanctions Bill, Sends It To Trump Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US representatives speak to journalists outside the US Capitol in Washington after the bill aiming to impose sanctions on Russia and Iran passed the House on September 16. WASHINGTON -- The US Congress on September 16 passed sweeping legislation targeting Russia and Iran, sending to President Donald Trump a sanctions package supporters say will increase pressure on Moscow and countries that help finance its war against Ukraine. The House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by a vote of 262-159, with 203 Republicans, 58 Democrats, and one independent voting in favor. Seven Republicans and 152 Democrats opposed it. The bill had already passed the Senate by an 86-11 vote last month. It is named for the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, who spent more than a year building bipartisan support for the legislation before his sudden death in July. Trump is expected to sign it. US Representative: Sanctions Legislation Will 'Cripple Putin's War Machine' by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:19 0:00 The legislation targets Russian officials, financial institutions, the energy sector, and the country's so-called shadow fleet of tankers. It also gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas and on countries that help Moscow evade sanctions. The measure also extends US sanctions on Iran. Its passage marks the first major bipartisan congressional legislation supporting Ukraine since an emergency aid package approved in April 2024. Tariffs Divide Democrats The bill's path through the House was complicated by Democratic opposition centered largely on the additional tariff authority given to Trump. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York said he supports pressuring Russia but could not support what he described as broad new presidential tariff powers. Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, likewise said he remained committed to stopping Russia's war against Ukraine but opposed the legislation's tariff provisions. Meeks said Trump already has substantial authority to sanction Moscow and argued that the bill should have included stronger requirements for the administration to use it. Fifty-eight Democrats nevertheless voted for the legislation, reflecting continued support among many lawmakers for imposing additional economic costs on Russia. Embed share Russian Drones Hit Ukrainian Passenger Train And Bus, Killing 5 by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:13 0:00 Direct link 240p | 2.3MB 360p | 3.1MB 480p | 4.5MB 720p | 7.4MB 1080p | 12.4MB Critics also raised concerns that the tariff powers could affect US partners and allies, including European countries that continue to import Russian energy. But European officials cited after the vote did not echo the broader argument that Europe opposed the legislation. Hannes Hanso, Estonia's ambassador to the United States, told RFE/RL on September 16 that Tallinn supports strong sanctions against Russia and wants them implemented quickly. "We support as strong sanctions as possible on Russia," Hanso said. "They are the aggressor, so this now enables very solid, strong, comprehensive sanctions." Hanso acknowledged that the legislation was not perfect but said the priority was putting the new sanctions into effect. "The sooner we can implement those sanctions against Russia the better," he said. SEE ALSO: Explosive-Laden Drone Shot Down Over Lithuania As Russia, Ukraine Trade Strikes The EU has maintained extensive sanctions against Russia, while European governments have continued to call for pressure on Moscow over its war against Ukraine. For Representative Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, the focus now shifts from congressional action to how the Trump administration uses the new powers. "We're going to pay close attention to the administration and to see what they're going to do with these new powers that have been given," Kaptur told RFE/RL. 'We Have Your Number' Supporters of the legislation say its tariff provisions are intended to target countries whose purchases of Russian energy help finance Moscow's war. Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, a Democratic co-author of the legislation, delivered a blunt message to the Kremlin after the vote. "To Vladimir Putin, we have your number," Blumenthal said. He warned China and India that continued purchases of Russian oil and gas could expose them to the new US measures. "China and India, you better clean up your act, buy your oil and gas somewhere else," he said. Blumenthal said the legislation was intended to increase pressure on Moscow and force Putin toward negotiations, while stressing that sanctions alone would not be enough. "Appeasement is not a strategy," he said, adding that Congress would need to continue providing Ukraine with military, economic and political support. SEE ALSO: A Quiet Ukrainian Counteroffensive, A 'Rout' For Russian Forces Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the measure sends an "unmistakable, bipartisan message" to Putin. "Every dollar Russia earns through illicit energy sales is another dollar Putin can use to buy drones, missiles, and weapons to kill innocent Ukrainians," Shaheen said. She urged Trump to sign the bill and use the new authorities to pressure Putin into "meaningfully" negotiating an end to the war. Republican Senator Katie Britt of Alabama, a key supporter of the legislation, said the measure would also hold Iran accountable for what she described as "47 years of terror." The bill extends the Iran Sanctions Act by five years, maintaining sanctions targeting Iran's energy and weapons sectors. A Tribute To Graham The vote also marked the culmination of a campaign led by Graham, who worked with Blumenthal and other senators to build bipartisan support for the legislation. Graham reached an agreement with the Trump administration shortly before his death that helped clear the way for the Senate vote. "This means so much to me and it meant so much to Lindsey," Graham's sister, Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina, said after the House vote. SEE ALSO: Ukrainian Lawmakers Approve Removal Of Prosecutor-General Amid New Scandal Representative Michael McCaul of Texas, who introduced the House version of the legislation, said the bill could significantly damage Russia's ability to finance its war. McCaul said it would "cripple Russia's war machine" and increase pressure on Putin to negotiate. "Lindsey understood these threats. He had the guts to stand up and confront them, no matter what the political cost was," McCaul said. "Today, 262 members of the House voted not just for Ukraine, but for freedom and democracy," he added. "And today, we are now one step closer to securing Lindsey's vision of enduring peace in Ukraine and beyond." House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana said the legislation puts "maximum pressure" on Putin and countries helping Russia evade sanctions. "For too long, Putin has bankrolled this devastating war with money and resources from countries willing to look the other way, and today, that ends," Johnson said. https://www.rferl.org/a/iran-women-life-.body: Iran Four Years On, Iranian Woman Seeks Justice For Brother Killed In Women, Life, Freedom Protests By RFE/RL's Radio Farda September 16, 2026 15:01 CET Four Years On, Iranian Woman Seeks Justice For Brother Killed In Women, Life, Freedom Protests Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A protest against Iran's clerical rulers outside the Iranian Embassy in Mexico City in 2022. Shahriar Mohammadi was among the hundreds killed in Iran's bloody crackdown on the Women, Life, Freedom protests that erupted four years ago. The nationwide demonstrations were triggered by the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a young woman who was accused of violating the country's controversial hijab law. The protests began as a rebuke of the brutal enforcement of the Islamic head scarf but grew into one of the most sustained challenges to Iran's clerical rulers, who used lethal force to crush the rallies, killing around 500 people, human rights groups said. Embed share Four Years After Mahsa Amini's Death, Iranian Women Defy Hijab Law by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:06 0:00 Direct link 240p | 4.2MB 360p | 5.7MB 480p | 8.2MB 720p | 13.2MB 1080p | 21.3MB Mohammadi was shot in the northwestern city of Bukan in November 2022. Iranian security forces fired on his vehicle, and the 28-year-old later died in hospital from his wounds, his family has said. "It's very difficult to put these four years into words," Asrin Mohammadi, his sister, told RFE/RL's Radio Farda. "Our lives were completely transformed and turned upside down." In their pursuit of justice for Mohammadi's death, his family found themselves on a collision course with the authorities. Iranian police detained and interrogated Asrin and her other brother, Milad, she said. They also barred the family from visiting Mohammadi's grave and holding any gatherings marking his death. "Because we sought justice, we were detained, tortured -- psychologically and physically -- and forced to emigrate," said Asrin. "These four years have been incredibly challenging, especially given the magnitude of the loss we experienced." 'Forced To Leave My Homeland' Asrin and her brother fled to Canada soon after they were released from detention, she said. "I had wanted to remain in Iran and ensure that something would be done so that the perpetrators would pay a price," said Asrin. "Unfortunately, they continued pursuing me and built a very serious case against me. I was therefore forced to leave my homeland." Even in exile, she and her brother have continued their fight for justice, working with leading human rights groups including Amnesty International to document human rights violations and build detailed case files. "I don't expect justice to be achieved overnight," said Asrin. "But I want everyone involved -- those who ordered the killings, those who carried out the repression, and those who fired the shots -- to one day be tried and held accountable in independent courts." SEE ALSO: Amini's Parents Pay Tribute To Daughter On Anniversary Of Death Amnesty International on September 16 released a more than 1,000-page report that accused Iranian authorities of committing crimes against humanity, murder, torture, enforced disappearance, imprisonment, rape, and persecution during the protests in 2022. Based on interviews with 270 people and analysis of over 2,000 videos, the report identified 87 Iranian officials that Amnesty International said should be investigated for crimes against humanity. The rights group said the authorities disproportionately targeted Iran's ethnic Kurdish and Baluch minorities "with lethal repression and subjected them to the crime against humanity of persecution." https://www.rferl.org/a/belarus-us-priso.body: Belarus Belarus Releases 25 Prisoners After Lukashenko's Latest Talks With US Envoy Coale By RFE/RL's Belarus Service September 16, 2026 13:55 CET Belarus Releases 25 Prisoners After Lukashenko's Latest Talks With US Envoy Coale Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Freed Belarusian political prisoners arrive in Lithuania on September 16. US special envoy John Coale announced that 25 people were released from Belarusian prisons in exchange for the lifting of US sanctions on two Belarusian companies following talks with the country’s longtime authoritarian leader, Aleksandr Lukashenko. “25 prisoners are free today!” Coale wrote on X on September 16. "We agreed to an interim deal, and as a show of goodwill Belarus will release 25 people and in exchange the United States will lift sanctions on two companies," he added in comments to reporters in the Belarusian capital, Minsk. Embed share Belarus Frees 25 Political Prisoners As US Says It Will Ease Sanctions by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:59 0:00 The US envoy has been negotiating with Lukashenko since last year, with the talks leading to the release of some 500 people in return for an easing of Washington’s sanctions against Belarus. In the latest such effort, the United States will lift its sanctions on Belarusian paint manufacturer Lakokraska and forestry sector group Bellesbumprom, Coale told the state news agency BelTA. The United States and the European Union hit Lukashenko and his government with major sanctions in the wake of the 2020 presidential election, in which Lukashenko, in power since 1994, claimed victory. Further restrictions were imposed in 2022 after Minsk allowed Moscow to use Belarusian territory as a launchpad for its invasion of Ukraine. SEE ALSO: Drama At The Border: How Belarusian Dissident Statkevich Refused Exile “We will continue to improve US-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future,” he wrote on X, having earlier told BelTA that “additional sanctions relief” would continue to be granted in exchange. Coale later told Reuters in an interview that he expects to return to Belarus in about one month's time, possibly to announce the release of many more prisoners. "I hope hundreds (are released). I don't know. That's my hope," Coale was quoted as saying. "I'm confident that we'll get a lot more out." Following the latest round of diplomacy, exiled Belarusian opposition leader Svyatlana Tsikhanouskaya wrote on X that she was “happy for every person who has finally found themselves free today” and “for their families and loved ones who have been waiting for this day.” John Coale and Belarus prisoners released on September 16. “Every person released is a victory. So today’s release is another humanitarian result,” she said, adding, however, that “it is far from the end of this process,” with hundreds of other prisoners remaining behind bars in Belarus. According to earlier estimates by the Viasna rights group, which monitors arrests and is banned in Belarus, the country was still holding more than 900 political prisoners, even as Washington negotiated the release of hundreds of detainees beginning in 2025. While Belarusian opposition figures have largely welcomed US efforts to secure the release of prisoners, experts say Lukashenko is using the issue to “legitimize” his rule internationally and is arresting more people to replace those freed, an assertion denied by the Belarusian leader during his talks with Coale in Minsk. “For Lukashenko, the most important thing is...strengthening his political agency,” Vadim Mozheiko, director of the Krakow-based Kosciuszko Institute, told Current Time on September 16, adding that this “is especially important given his lack of domestic legitimacy.” Separately, Mozheiko pointed out that a “significant proportion of those released were forcibly deported from Belarus,” a move he described as “yet another form of repression.” A September 15 report by the UN experts said that "Belarusian authorities are using the country’s criminal justice system as an instrument of repression, systematically targeting and persecuting individuals deemed to oppose the government." "Plainclothes officers routinely detain individuals they label as critical of the Government without warrants, subject them to beatings and stress positions, deny access to lawyers, and force them to record humiliating 'repentance' videos under duress and threats against their families," it added. SEE ALSO: Belarusian State Quietly Builds Dissident DNA Database After Coale released a picture of the people freed on September 16, RFE/RL’s Belarus Service identified several prominent figures among them who had been arrested amid Belarus’s crackdown on anti-government protests and in the years that followed. Among them was Lyudmila Chekina, the director-general of Belarus’s popular news portal Tut.by, which was shut down amid pressure from the country’s authorities in 2021. She was sentenced to 12 years in prison on various charges, including “harming the national security of the Republic of Belarus.” Paval Belavus, a noted art manager and founder of a popular shop selling Belarusian national symbols, was also released. He had previously been sentenced to 13 years in prison on high treason and other charges. With reporting by Reuters and Current Time. https://www.rferl.org/a/serbia-china-mil.body: Serbia Serbia Reveals Armed Robot Dogs Days After Chinese Humanoid Factory Opening September 16, 2026 17:46 CET By Amos Chapple Photo: Serbian Army (Courtesy Image) Serbia Serbia Reveals Armed Robot Dogs Days After Chinese Humanoid Factory Opening September 16, 2026 17:46 CET By Amos Chapple Serbia Reveals Armed Robot Dogs Days After Chinese Humanoid Factory Opening Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Two weeks after Serbia opened a factory producing Chinese-designed robots, the Serbian military has shown armed quadruped robots operating alongside soldiers in a major military exercise. The September 13 use of the robots came after Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic vowed on August 29 that armed Chinese-designed robots serving in Belgrade's military would be seen "within 15 days" of the opening of the robot factory in Sabac, western Serbia. The armed quadrupeds resemble the D1 Max Pro, an industrial robot made by Chinese company AgiBot, which is a partner in the Sabac factory. But it remains unclear whether the robots shown at the exercise were assembled in Serbia. The Serbian military did not respond to a question from RFE/RL on where the robot dogs were produced. A robot dog seen during the Victor 2026 military exercise The quadrapeds from the Victor 2026 military exercise in southwestern Serbia were reportedly armed with Yugoslav-designed Wasp anti-tank missiles, automatic rifles, and 40mm grenade launchers. The images show the quadrupeds firing an automatic weapon and entering a dummy building as soldiers swarm alongside. With the Sabac robotics factory aiming to produce 3,000 humanoid and quadruped robots annually, the military exercise images have raised the specter of armies of killer robot dogs emerging from the Balkans. But that appears unlikely anytime soon, according to observers. "Serbia will likely encounter the same issues that have prompted militaries to reconsider their adoption of robot dogs," Jared Keller , a US-based weapons technology expert, told RFE/RL. "Compared to other unmanned platforms, quadrupeds still require significant development" to overcome issues around reliability and range, he added. Quadruped robots are seen entering dummy buildings during the Serbian military exercise. Ukraine's military received widespread publicity after posting about the use of robot dogs by its soldiers in August 2024. But in the two years since, the robots have rarely been seen on the battlefield. Over the same period, wheeled ground drones have been widely adopted by frontline troops. A representative from Brave1, the Ukrainian initiative behind many of the country's battlefield innovations, told RFE/RL that wheeled drones "may be preferable [over quadruped robots] for some missions because of their payload, endurance, and because they can be used for long-range missions." Brave1 did not directly respond to a question about whether quadruped robots had been phased out of Ukraine's war effort, but said that "legged platforms may offer advantages in difficult terrain or around obstacles." SEE ALSO: Serbia Deepens Military Ties With China Through Drones, Air Defense Systems A wheeled Ukrainian Spider ground drone used in the country's military weighs 50 kilograms but is capable of carrying a payload of a 100 kilograms. In comparison, an advanced quadruped robot weighing the same as the spider is able to carry just 10 kilograms. Belgrade has claimed its "robodog" has a maximum payload of 50 kilograms. Robot dogs are far more mechanically complex than wheeled drones, with around 12 individual motors needed in each quadruped, along with a complex suite of sensors. Such mechanical complexity drains batteries, increases the chances of breakdowns, and adds to the cost of the technology. Advanced quadrupeds cost tens of thousand of dollars and would be easy targets for cheap first-person-view attack drones. A wounded resident of the Ukrainian city of Druzhkivka is evacuated on a ground drone in July. Serbia's unveiling of the killer quadruped technology comes amid Belgrade's increasing incorporation of advanced Chinese weapons systems into its military's arsenal, including missile systems and aerial drones. N early 60 percent of Serbia's weapons imports from 2020-2024 were from China. Both the European Union and the United States have hinted at increasing unease over what Beijing and Belgrade refer to as their "steel friendship." A US State Department spokesperson told RFE/RL's Balkan Service that "Serbia's future economic opportunities will depend largely on the investments, policy decisions, and partnership choices it makes today." The spokesperson further called for Belgrade to choose "trusted sources and suppliers of AI equipment and technology" and to choose "reliable partners like the United States." Keller says Serbia's public display of killer quadrupeds may be more about geopolitical optics than real-world battle strategy. "Middle-tier leaders frequently trot out advanced weaponry to telegraph technological prowess, even when those systems are not often backed up by the defined tactics and doctrine that are the foundation for real-world operations," he said.
