This sweeping crackdown has nothing to do with protecting families and everything to do with further stigmatizing a community that has battled decades of discrimination Esther Major, Amnesty International “This appalling escalation in Türkiye’s crackdown amounts to a full-scale assault on LGBTI rights and those who defend them. The relentless raids, arrests and demonization of LGBTI people under the spurious guise of ‘protecting the families’ demonstrates why defending LGBTI rights in Türkiye is more important than ever,” said Esther Major, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe. “This sweeping crackdown, in which scores of people have been arrested, has nothing to do with protecting families and everything to do with further harming and stigmatizing a community that has battled decades of discrimination and intimidation.” As protest within Türkiye builds and international condemnation mounts, it is clear that the Turkish authorities have every intention of intensifying the crackdown. On Monday, the Ministry of Justice sent a circular to 175 chief public prosecutors in all of Türkiye’s 81 provinces, regarding content and activities deemed in their view contrary to “public morality” and harmful to families, children and young people. On the same day, police reportedly used pepper spray against peaceful protesters in İzmir. Two protesters were detained and later released. Earlier today, police surrounded a group of peaceful protestors that had gathered outside the İstanbul Courthouse in Çağlayan before they were able to deliver their press statement. More than 95 people were reportedly detained. Amnesty International is calling on authorities to allow further countrywide protests to take place without undue restriction. It is time to stand together against the repression of LGBTI rights in Türkiye, to raise our voices and to make our solidarity visible Esther Major, Amnesty International “The sweeping crackdown is part of a wider ongoing attack on the rights of LGBTI people and those who advocate for LGBTI rights. Amnesty International urges Turkish authorities end this wave of repression, ensure the immediate release of all those detained solely for their human rights work and guarantee that LGBTI defenders and associations can exercise their rights without discrimination, criminalization, intimidation or reprisals,” said Esther Major. “Everyone has the right to live free from discrimination, and we must take action to challenge this unjustifiable crackdown. On Friday, Amnesty International will join thousands taking to the streets of capital cities across the world to show our solidarity with LGBTI people in Türkiye. It is time to stand together against the repression of LGBTI rights in Türkiye, to raise our voices and to make our solidarity visible.” Background The raids on 12 September were carried out under the name “Ailem Güvende” (“My Family Is Safe”) and coordinated by the chief public prosecutor’s offices of Ankara, İstanbul, İzmir, Aydın and Mersin. The circular issued by the Ministry of Justice instructs prosecutors to promptly assess complaints and reports, take immediate investigative steps, preserve digital evidence and, where necessary, seek the removal or blocking of online content. On Friday 18 September, Amnesty International will be joining international protests outside Turkish embassies in capital cities around the world, including Brussels, Paris, London, Oslo, Washington DC and many more. Amnesty International Türkiye received an email from X on 14 September informing it that its X account (@aforgutu) had been blocked, following a decision communicated by the Cyber Security Presidency under Article 8/A of Law No. 5651. The account remains accessible outside of the country. Amnesty Türkiye has contacted X to request a copy of the decision but has yet to receive it, which means it cannot scrutinize the legal basis for the measure. Amnesty Türkiye’s new X account: @amnestyTR . On 13 September, Amnesty International was part of a joint statement by the Solidarity Network for Human Rights Defenders condemning the criminalization of LGBTI rights in Türkiye, and calling for the immediate and unconditional release of those detained, as well as an end to the targeting and pressure against LGBTI people, organizations and human rights defenders.

On 16 September 2026, the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen will give her annual State of the European Union address. Here, Caroline Hansen, EU Foreign Policy Advocate at Amnesty International, and Claudio Francavilla, Associate Director for EU Advocacy, for Human Rights Watch, write that this year’s speech must be an opportunity to make good on past promises and finally present a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements. Last year’s “State of the European Union” speech made headlines when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen finally proposed suspending the trade part of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and sanctioning Israeli ministers and settlers. One year on, almost none of those measures have been adopted, and as more and more EU countries and allies adopt bans on trade with Israel’s illegal settlements , von der Leyen’s Europe is lagging behind. These failures come with consequences: not only for her own credibility and that of the EU, but most of all for the lives of millions displaced, killed or wounded in Palestine and across the region. Von der Leyen should use this year’s address to remedy that, by firstly making good on last year’s proposals, then by ensuring the EU joins the ranks of those banning trade with Israel’s illegal settlements. Proposals with no follow up Von der Leyen’s proposals last year came only after an official declaration of famine in the Gaza Strip, where Israeli authorities unlawfully blocked humanitarian aid as part of their genocidal campaign Her proposals followed mass protests across Europe demanding an end to EU inaction and complicity, and calls by several EU member states and civil society groups to suspend the EU-Israel Association Agreement, whose essential human rights clause the EU found to have been breached by Israel. “It truly pains me to say these words”, she confessed before announcing her proposals , which also included targeted sanctions against “extremist” Israeli ministers and settlers, and a suspension of a few million euros worth of EU funding to Israeli projects. But there she stopped. As Germany and Italy obstructed the suspension of the Agreement and Hungary and Czechia vetoed sanctions against Israeli ministers, von der Leyen was reticent to speak out, in stark contrast to her approach on Hungary’s repeated vetoes on EU sanctions against Russia. And while the EU repeated its condemnations of Israel’s illegal settlements, von der Leyen resisted growing calls to introduce a ban on the EU trade fueling the settlements’ economy and related abuses . Von der Leyen also remained silent as Israel’s foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar lashed out at EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, nor did she comment when EU Commissioner Dubravka Šuica met him in Tel Aviv shortly after , exposing a growing division and lack of solidarity in her Commission mirroring those among EU states. As Europe showed weakness, divisions and its inability to deliver more than a handful of sanctions against Israeli settlers, the situation in the region kept deteriorating. Israel’s spiralling abuses When von der Leyen’s delivered her 2025 speech, at least 64,000 Palestinians had been killed in the Gaza Strip. That number is now close to 74,000 despite a so-called “ceasefire” in force since October 2025. Israeli authorities continue to impose severe, arbitrary and unlawful aid restrictions as they have confined the population into approximately 30 percent of the territory, and are once again openly discussing plans to ethnically cleanse Gaza of its Palestinian population. In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, despite protests by the EU and other close allies , Israeli authorities have turbocharged the expansion of illegal settlements. This resulted in expedited home demolitions, land seizure, fragmentation and dispossession of Palestinians – hallmarks of Israel’s ethnic cleansing and apartheid against Palestinians. At least 88 Palestinians, including 22 children, have been killed in the West Bank this year alone, bringing the total since October 2023 to nearly 1,100. Israeli authorities also adopted a death penalty bill that de facto applies to Palestinians only and continue to detain thousands of Palestinians without charges or trial, including doctors like Hussam Abu Safiya , subjecting many to systematic torture . In Lebanon, despite ceasefires that went into effect on April 17 and June 20, Israeli attacks have killed at least 4,383 people since the beginning of the March 2026 escalation, including 261 children, 399 women, and 135 medical workers, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry. Israeli forces continue to cause widespread destruction and mass displacement, committing acts that Amnesty International has found to constitute war crimes. Von der Leyen’s responsibilities As President of the European Commission, von der Leyen has the duty to ensure that all EU policies – including its policies on trade and foreign affairs – comply with international law. She can’t hide behind the EU’s humanitarian aid to Palestinians while doing nothing to address the reasons why such aid is so desperately needed. Nor can she blame member states for not approving her half-hearted proposals: she should actively and vocally engage with them and urge them to comply with the legal obligations under the UN Genocide Convention. By the time of last year’s speech, Amnesty International , Al-Haq , B’Tselem , UN experts , and the International Association of Genocide Scholars were among those who had already concluded Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. Shortly after, a UN independent Commission of Inquiry confirmed those findings. But whether von der Leyen agrees with the genocide qualification is irrelevant: under the Genocide Convention, awareness of a “serious risk” of genocide triggers the “duty to prevent” , compelling all states parties to that treaty – including all EU states – to “employ all means reasonably available to them, so as to prevent genocide so far as possible”. For the EU, that means suspending the Association Agreement and sanctioning Israeli officials. Von der Leyen should also reaffirm the EU’s commitment to international justice and propose the use of the EU blocking statute to protect the International Criminal Court and those cooperating with it from crippling sanctions , adopted by the US as part of its campaign to dismantle the Court and shield its own and Israeli officials from accountability. Von der Leyen should use this speech to propose an EU-wide ban of trade with Israel’s illegal settlements Much as she did with the Association Agreement, she doesn’t need preemptive support by the EU Council. No matter how much it might “pain” her, she should put the proposal on the table, and actively engage with member states, especially Germany and Italy, to ensure she has the necessary qualified majority to approve a measure that is required by international law . Amid global turmoil and instability, Europe and the world desperately need principled, committed leaders determined to uphold the rules, especially those devised to prevent, punish and redress the worst atrocities, and adopt all necessary measures to that end. For the EU, another year of failures, inaction and half-hearted proposals is blow to its credibility. For Palestinians and so many others in the region, it’s a matter of life and death. What you can do to help Suspend EU-Israel Trade Agreement Send a message and demand the leaders of Germany and Italy support suspending the EU’s trade agreement with Israel. There is no time to lose. Algeria’s authorities must immediately abandon any plans to expand the scope of the death penalty or resume executions after more than three decades without carrying one out, said Amnesty International as the government examines amendments to the penal code that would broaden the use of the death penalty. The organization calls on Algeria’s authorities to immediately establish an official moratorium as a first step towards fully abolishing the death penalty. It also urges the authorities to adopt a human-rights centred response to the recent devastating wildfires, including by ensuring effective investigations into all factors that led to the tragic loss of life and accountability without resort to the death penalty. On 30 August, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune instructed the Minister of Justice to amend the Penal Code by 15 September to “reintroduce” the death penalty for intentionally starting or instigating fires. He stressed that anyone sentenced to death would face execution as soon as they have exhausted their right of appeal. The directive came in the wake of deadly wildfires that erupted between 26 and 30 August, wiping out entire villages across the Kabylie region and other parts of northeastern Algeria. On 6 September, the government started examining the proposed draft amendments to the Penal Code and the president indicated that they would further introduce the death penalty for “child abductors and abusers”. “The devastation and loss of life caused by these fires is a profound tragedy and should spur the Algerian authorities into taking immediate steps focusing both on prevention and accountability. But walking back from over 30 years without executions is a deeply retrograde response that runs counter to respect for the right to life,” said Nadege Lahmar, Algeria Researcher. “It is also at odd with Algeria’s international human rights obligations, in addition to its consistent support to UN General Assembly resolutions calling for a moratorium on executions with a view to abolishing the death penalty.” Amnesty International considers the death penalty to be a violation of the right to life and the ultimate cruel, inhuman, and degrading punishment; which does not have a unique deterrent effect on crime and perpetuates a cycle of violence. In addition to drawing from previous research into politically motivated trials in Algeria, Amnesty International reviewed public statements from the Algerian government as well as media reports since the eruption of the fires and analyzed relevant legal provisions relating to arson. On 7 September Amnesty International shared its concerns and recommendations with the Algerian authorities. No response has been received at the time of writing. Wildfires should not be used to justify repression The Algerian government has not shared comprehensive figures of deaths and injuries from the fires. Official government figures on 26 August recorded 12 deaths and 54 hospitalizations , but credible sources have since reported significantly higher casualties , including over 70 deaths in a single municipality . In July, separate wildfires killed six people also in the northeast. While authorities linked the July fires to a severe heatwave and previously described wildfires as a major risk and structural challenge exacerbated by climate change, in August, the Algerian president pointed to the responsibility of criminal elements “attempting to weaken Algeria and undermine its unity”. Between 26 July and 10 September , the authorities announced the detentions of 20 people pending investigations for arson and “subversion” – a terrorism-related charge punished by a mandatory death penalty. They claimed a supporter of the Movement for the Self-determination of Kabylie (MAK), a political opposition group which the Algerian authorities designated as “terrorist”, was among those detained. Algerian authorities have previously used wildfires to justify repression and resort to the death penalty. Following the August 2021 wildfires in northeastern Algeria, which killed at least 90 people, the authorities blamed political opposition groups, primarily the MAK, and prosecuted scores of people on terrorism-related and other serious charges. In November 2022, a court convicted and sentenced 56 people to death in a mass trial marred by gross fair trial violations and torture allegations that were not investigated; at least 10 among them were sentenced to death based on their political affiliations. The Supreme Court subsequently ordered a retrial, which commenced on 1 March 2026. Courts have also resorted to politically motivated terrorism-related charges sanctioned by death to prosecute peaceful activists in at least two other cases unrelated to wildfires since 2021. This record makes the proposed expansion of the death penalty all the more alarming. Need for a human rights-centred response As Algeria faces increasingly frequent and severe wildfires in the context of worsening global heating due to climate change, the authorities should focus on protecting lives, strengthening prevention and emergency response – including by addressing the root causes of climate exacerbated disasters, and ensuring credible investigations and accountability. “Accountability for the devastating loss of life caused by wildfires cannot be reduced to pursuing alleged perpetrators of arson. Authorities must conduct thorough, independent, impartial, and transparent investigations into all factors that caused or contributed to the fires and loss of life, including any failures by public officials and shortcomings in prevention, preparedness and emergency response,” said Nadege Lahmar. “The findings must be made public and where there is sufficient evidence of criminal responsibility, those responsible must be prosecuted in fair proceedings that exclude resort to the death penalty. Survivors and families also have a right to timely, accessible and accurate information regarding those missing or deceased.” Background Under current Algerian law, arson carries penalties ranging from three years to life imprisonment and the death penalty if it causes death. Although Algeria has not carried out executions since 1993, courts continue to impose death sentences most commonly for murder . In July 2025, authorities already broadened the scope of the death penalty to include several drug-related offences . Algeria is party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) which restricts the use of the death penalty to the “most serious crimes”, interpreted as offences involving intentional killing; and sets its abolition as a goal in countries that still retain this cruel punishment. In line with Article 6 of the ICCPR, the UN Human Rights Committee stated that “state parties may not transform into a capital offence any offence that, upon ratification of the [ICCPR] or at any time thereafter, did not entail the death penalty” nor should they increase its application. Amnesty International opposes the death penalty unconditionally, in all cases and under any circumstances.

https://kloop.kg/blog/2026/09/15/25-mln-.body: Facebook Twitter VK Telegram WhatsApp Государство «неэффективно» выдало кредит в $25 млн топливной компании приближенного экс-главы ГКНБ Камчыбека Ташиева — заявила Счетная палата. Фирма принадлежит Акылбеку Маматову — его семья уже 10 лет, выигрывает гостендеры на поставку топлива. Акылбек Маматов По данным аудитора Счетной палаты Алимжана Байгазакова, в 2025 году кабмин выдал компании Маматова «Альфа Ойл» (сеть АЗС Red Petroleum) кредит в $25 млн под 7%. Это было сделано в рамках госпрограммы по сдерживанию цен на ГСМ. Цены на топливо в Кыргызстане растут из-за нехватки бензина, связанной с украинскими атаками на российские НПЗ. А потом государство само же погасило проценты по этому займу. «Кредит был выдан под 7 процентов. Эти 7 процентов мы полностью покрыли за счет государства. То есть они получили деньги, фактически не оплачивая кредитную ставку», — сказал Байгазаков, выступая в парламенте. Алимжан Байгазаков При этом в качестве залога под кредит было передано не имущество «Альфа Ойл», а активы Государственного финансового холдинга на сумму $250 тысяч. То есть, если компания не выплатит кредит вовремя, его должно будет погашать государство. В противном случае госфинхолдинг потеряет свое имущество. По данным аудитора Счетной палаты, объем ГСМ, поставляемый «Альфа Ойл», составляет всего 12-13 процентов от рынка и компания «не внесла какого-то значительного вклада в стабильность цен». «А на вопрос: Почему нашли именно „Альфа Ойл“ и дали ей деньги? — до сегодняшнего дня они [кабмин] так и не смогли ответить», — добавил Байгазаков. В ответ на критику, «Альфа Ойл» заявила , что по итогам 2025 года она контролировала около 40% рынка и успешно использовала кредит, что позволило избежать дефицита топлива на их заправках. Позиция компании изначально была опубликована на сайте информагентства 24.kg , но позже публикацию удалили. Предложение о выдаче кредита «Альфа Ойл» было выдвинуто Министерством Финансов и Министерством Экономики, а постановление подписано кабмином. Правительство пока никак не прокомментировала выводы аудитора Счетной палаты. Еще один кредит Но это еще не все. 28 апреля 2026 года парламентский комитет по финансам, бюджету, предпринимательству и развитию конкуренции одобрил распоряжении кабмина о выдаче «Альфа Ойл» кредита на $36 млн. Тоже под 7% со льготным периодом 21 месяц. П оручителем снова выступил Государственный финансовый холдинг. «Если [ «Альфа ойл» ] вовремя не выплатят [госкредит с процентами], мы [государство] должны будем это сделать», — объясняла замминистра финансов Жибек Дуйшеева. Жибек Дуйшеева За две недели до этого владельца «Альфа Ойл» Акылбека Маматова задержали по подозрению в «злоупотреблении должностным положением». И хотя 20 апреля его отпустили под подписку о невыезде, публично правоохранительные органы пока не объявляли о закрытии уголовного дела, по которому он проходит. Не смотря на это з амминистра экономики и коммерции Беназир Нурланова заверила, что выдать кредит необходимо для топливно-экономической безопасности страны и комитет его одобрил. Приближенный Ташиева Акылбек Маматов торгует топливом в розницу на АЗС Red Petroleum и считается близким к опальному экс-главе ГКНБ Камчыбеку Ташиеву . Маматов входит в Исполком Кыргызского футбольного союза, который до апреля 2026 года возглавлял Ташиев. В 2024 году семья Ташиева продала Маматову свою нефтебазу в Жалал-Абаде. А в Оше Маматов начал продавать ГСМ на заправках бизнесмена Жалила Атамбаева, задержанного подчиненными тогда еще главы спецслужб Ташиева. Абдимуктар Маматов С экс-главой ГКНБ был связан не только Акылбек Маматов, но и его отец Абдимуктар. В прошлом он был акимом Сузакского района — малой родины Камчыбека Ташиева. А зимой 2026 года Маматов-старший стал одним из подписантов скандального « письма 75 », где влиятельные лица в завуалированной форме предлагали президенту Садыру Жапарову уступить место Ташиеву. Некоторые подписанты после этого были задержаны , а Ташиев был снят со всех должностей и осужден за попытку захвата власти. В сентябре горсуд Бишкека переквалифицировал обвинение в «Воспрепятствование осуществлению избирательных прав» и приговорил Ташиева и других подсудимых к четырем годам лишения свободы с применением пробации на два года. Конфликт интересов Семья Маматовых была связана с властью и до возвышения Ташиева. С 2010 по 2020 год Абдимуктар Маматов был членом парламентских Комитетов по денежно-кредитной политике и ТЭК. В этот период компания его сына Акылбека заключила более 3900 госконтрактов на поставки топлива, выручив более 1 млрд сомов. Э то был явный конфликт интересов: по закону о госзакупках компании Маматова-младшего не имели права торговать с государством, поскольку его отец занимал высшую политическую должность. Но Маматовым это сошло с рук. Как и дело 2012 года о контрабанде ГСМ, в которой Маматова-младшего обвиняло ГКНБ. Тогда, по данным чекистов, он признал вину и выплатил государству 22 млн сомов. ЭТО МОЖЕТ БЫТЬ ИНТЕРЕСНО ЕЩЕ ОТ АВТОРА Медведь в объятиях дракона. https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2.body: By Naomi Bernaldez, Campaigner on Amnesty International’s Central America team Naomi took part in the Write for Rights campaign for Juan López and created a collage using fragments from more than 15,000 letters sent from around the world. In this article, she reflects on what it meant to carry a sample of that solidarity to Honduras and to meet Juan’s family and fellow activists. Defending water cost him his life Juan López was a Honduran father, husband, human rights defender and environmental activist. Since 2015, together with other members of the community of Tocoa, he had defended the Guapinol and San Pedro rivers, the forests and Carlos Escaleras Mejía National Park against mining and energy projects that threatened the ecosystem and water quality. Juan and his colleagues founded the Tocoa Municipal Committee for the Defence of Common and Public Goods to peacefully challenge the legality of these projects. As a result of their activism, members of the Committee have faced threats, harassment, criminalization and attacks. On 14 September 2024, Juan was killed as he was leaving a church in Tocoa. His death left an irreparable void for his family and community... That is why Juan’s story was selected for Write for Rights, Amnesty International’s global campaign that mobilizes millions of people every year to stand in solidarity with those who have suffered human rights violations. A message that travelled thousands of kilometres The campaign for Juan generated 332,381 actions worldwide. In June, I travelled with several colleagues to Tegucigalpa to deliver a message that had already travelled thousands of kilometres before we did. In our suitcases, we carried just a fraction of those actions. It was something immense: a selection from more than 15,000 letters of solidarity written for Juan’s family, his colleagues from the Committee and the Justice for the Peoples Law Firm, which represents them legally. For months, I had watched these letters arrive, one after another, and had witnessed the care, hope and commitment contained in every word. Even so, it was not until I held a selection of those messages on the way to Honduras that I fully grasped what they really meant. I thought about the thousands of people who had taken a few minutes out of their lives to write a message or draw something for someone they had never met. In a world that so often seems marked by indifference, those letters were proof that empathy can still cross borders. As the campaign progressed, I felt the need to find a way to represent all the solidarity arriving from different parts of the world. That is how a collage made from fragments of the letters came about. As I created it, I discovered something deeply moving. Although every letter was unique, they all shared the same intention: to stand alongside Juan’s family and colleagues, to express admiration for his legacy, and in many cases simply to let them know that people in different corners of the world were with them. The collage became far more than a visual piece; it became a representation of the strength of collective solidarity and a bridge connecting thousands of people. Although every letter was unique, they all shared the same intention: to stand alongside Juan’s family and colleagues, to express admiration for his legacy, and in many cases simply to let them know that people in different corners of the world were with them. However, the true meaning of the letters and the collage only came to life when we met in Honduras with the people they were intended for. It was then that I understood that what we were carrying was more than paper and ink: these were thousands of voices joining their struggle, honouring Juan’s history of resistance and reminding them that, even from thousands of kilometres away, there are people who believe in justice and stand alongside them. The handover was deeply emotional. It was not possible to physically carry all 15,000 letters in a single trip, but we could share a small part of the immense movement of solidarity that had grown around their cause. The day continued at the Legal Office for Indigenous Peoples, where we installed a mural in tribute to the struggle that Juan López represented. We then held a brief gathering with members of the Committee. It was a simple moment, but a deeply meaningful one. No grand speeches were needed. The memory, commitment and determination of those who have sustained this struggle for years could be felt in every conversation, every embrace and every look. I remember looking at the newly installed mural, the letters, the collage and the people gathered around them. At that moment, I understood something that we sometimes risk forgetting in our day-to-day work: campaigns do not end when an action is sent. Behind every letter is a person who chose to dedicate their time, attention and hope to someone else. And when those messages reach their destination, solidarity stops being an abstract idea and becomes something tangible. By the end of the day, I felt that we had travelled there to give something, but that we were returning having received far more. We came away with a lesson in perseverance, community and humanity. We learned that something as simple as writing a letter can become a source of strength for people facing enormous challenges. The more than 15,000 letters received, the collage created from their words and the mural installed in Honduras are different expressions of the same truth: solidarity has the power to cross borders, languages and distances. And when thousands of people decide to act together, no struggle has to be fought alone. Justice for Juan has still not been achieved, and more people are needed to raise their voices to demand an immediate, independent and impartial investigation into his killing, and for everyone responsible to be brought to justice in fair trials. I INVITE YOU TO ADD YOUR SUPPORT. DEMAND JUSTICE FOR JUAN LÓPEZ

Amnesty International welcomes the Guatemalan judiciary’s decision to close the criminal proceedings against four Indigenous authorities charged with unlawful association, terrorism, obstruction of justice, sedition and obstruction of criminal prosecution following their participation in peaceful protests during the national strike in October 2023. The ruling concerns Luis Pacheco, Héctor Chaclán and Basilio Puac, from the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán, and Esteban Toc, from the Indigenous Mayor’s Office of Sololá, who faced unfounded criminal proceedings in retaliation for their work defending human rights and the rule of law. “This unfounded prosecution and all the human rights violations it led to should never have happened. Luis Pacheco and Héctor Chaclán should never have been imprisoned. This ruling is a first step towards ending the arbitrary actions against them,” said Astrid Valencia, Amnesty International’s Deputy Research Director for the Americas. Luis Pacheco and Héctor Chaclán should never have been imprisoned. This ruling is a first step towards ending the arbitrary actions against them.” Astrid Valencia, Amnesty International’s Deputy Research Director for the Americas. In May 2026, Amnesty International named Luis Pacheco and Héctor Chaclán prisoners of conscience. They spent more than 15 months in pretrial detention, unjustly separated from their families and communities. The organization also warned about the misuse of criminal offences to punish Indigenous Peoples’ forms of organization and deter them from exercising their rights to peaceful protest and freedom of expression, in violation of international human rights standards. “The criminalization of Indigenous authorities for participating in peaceful demonstrations not only affects those accused, but also threatens Indigenous Peoples’ forms of community organization and systems of representation in Guatemala. We urge the Guatemalan authorities to ensure that no one is again subjected to arbitrary criminal proceedings for peacefully exercising their rights,” added Astrid Valencia. “The criminalization of Indigenous authorities for participating in peaceful demonstrations not only affects those accused, but also threatens Indigenous Peoples’ forms of community organization and systems of representation in Guatemala.” Astrid Valencia, Amnesty International’s Deputy Research Director for the Americas. Finally, we call on the authorities to ensure that Luis, Héctor, Basilio and Esteban receive full reparation for the harm caused to them, their families and communities. This must include ensuring that those suspected of responsibility for misusing the criminal justice system to harass them are investigated and prosecuted. For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact [email protected] .

https://cpj.org/2026/09/cpj-partners-urg.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email New York, September 15, 2026—The Committee to Protect Journalists and partner organizations call on the Chinese authorities to ensure journalist Sophia Huang Xueqin is freed without any arbitrary restrictions, as she approaches the end of a five-year prison sentence. Huang, whose reporting on human rights and sexual abuse helped spark China’s #MeToo movement, is due to be released on September 18 after serving a prison term on the charge of “inciting subversion of state power.” “Sophia Huang Xueqin should never have spent a day in jail,” said CPJ Asia-Pacific Director Beh Lih Yi. “Her unjust imprisonment exposes the insecurity of China — a government that is afraid of independent journalism and women who dare to speak truth to power. The Chinese authorities must guarantee her full freedom, without any further delay or arbitrary restrictions.” In a joint statement on Tuesday, CPJ was among 60 press freedom and human rights organizations that urged the Chinese government to ensure Huang is released immediately on Friday and guarantee that she could return to reporting without being subjected to surveillance, retaliation, or other forms of restrictions . Police detained Huang and a friend, labor activist Wang Jianbing, on September 19, 2021, while they were on their way to an airport in southern China. Huang was due to fly to Britain to study at the University of Sussex. Wang was jailed three and a half years on the same charge and was freed last year after completing the sentence. China consistently ranks as the world’s worst jailer of journalists, with at least 50 journalists behind bars, according to CPJ’s latest research . https://cpj.org/2026/09/cpj-calls-on-ice.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Mexico City, September 15, 2026—The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on U.S. immigration authorities to release Nicaraguan journalist Luis Galeano, director of the radio and internet program Café con Voz , who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents on the morning of September 14 in Orlando, Florida. Galeano was detained while driving for Uber, his wife, Deykel Santamaría, told the Nicaraguan news outlet Confidencial. While being transported to a police station, he was able to call her and ask her to contact his lawyer and notify journalists of his detention. “This detention fits into a troubling pattern in which the Trump administration has wielded immigration enforcement against members of the press,” said CPJ Américas Regional Director José Zamora, based in Miami. “It is critical that journalists who have sought asylum in the United States after fleeing persecution for their journalistic work are protected, not treated as targets for immigration enforcement.” Galeano fled Nicaragua in 2018 under the Ortega government’s crackdown on independent media and has directed Café con Voz from exile since then. In February 2023, he was among 94 Nicaraguans stripped of their citizenship by the Ortega government, which accused them of being “traitors to the homeland” and ordered the confiscation of their assets. CPJ has extensively documented Nicaragua’s press freedom crisis , which has driven an estimated 268 Nicaraguan journalists into exile , many of them settling in neighboring Costa Rica. Galeano is being held in the Florida Baker correctional facility in Sanderson Florida and is waiting for a hearing scheduled for October 2nd, according to Nicaraguan news website La Prensa . ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment. https://cpj.org/2026/09/turkey-arrests-j.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Istanbul, September 15, 2026—Turkish authorities must release arrested journalist Selahattin Günday without delay and stop abusing the country’s laws to harass journalists and prevent them from doing their jobs, the Committee to Protect Journalists said Tuesday. Günday , a former broadcast reporter for the now closed Doğan News Agency (DHA), was taken into custody by Istanbul police on September 10 as part of a newly reopened investigation into the death of Turkish intelligence operative Kaşif Kozinoğlu in 2011. On September 12, Günday was arrested on suspicion of exposing an intelligence operative and illegally obtaining personal data while reporting on Kozinoğlu in 2011, his lawyer Hüseyin Ersöz told local media. Journalist Selahattin Günday (left) and his lawyer Hüzeyin Ersöz. (Screenshot: KRT/YouTube) Camera operator İdris Tiftikçi, who worked with Günday at DHA, was also taken into custody on September10 but he was released pending trial under judicial control. “The arrest of journalist Selahattin Günday defies logic: how could he be involved in any way in the death of Kaşif Kozinoğlu, a jailed man he never met?” said Özgür Öğret, CPJ’s Turkey representative. “The authorities must release Günday immediately and stop harassing the press.” Kozinoğlu, who worked for the National Intelligence Agency ((MİT), was arrested in March 2011 and died in prison in November that same year, just days before he was due to testify in the Ergenekon trials, a series of court cases against individuals, including journalists , accused by the authorities of plotting to overthrow the government in a military coup. According to reports in local media , the accusations against Günday and Tiftikçi relate to their coverage of Kozinoğlu’s appearance at a court in Istanbul after his arrest, with authorities claiming they were the first to broadcast the news in violation of a law relating to publishing information about MİT or its officers. Ersöz said on social media on September 15 that he had objected to the arrest warrant and expected a decision on this objection to be made within days. He previously said the arrest was made under Article 27 of the MİT law, which was altered in 2014 to ban exposing the identities of intelligence operatives, and that in any case the statute of limitations had already passed for the alleged offences. “An arrest warrant was issued for an act that was not a crime at the time but, in any case, had ‘lapsed under the 15-year statute of limitations,’” Ersöz wrote on X. CPJ emailed the Chief Prosecutor’s Office of Istanbul for comment but did not receive a reply. https://cpj.org/2026/09/cpj-condemns-isr.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Israeli authorities to immediately end threats of legal action against Israeli journalist and filmmaker Yuval Abraham and filmmaker Rachel Szor over their documentary “ NAZA ,” which accuses the Israeli military of using AI-powered targeting systems in the mass killing of civilians in Gaza. Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar has threatened to seek the revocation of Abraham’s and Szor’s Israeli citizenship under the country’s Citizenship Law, saying it “allows for the revocation of citizenship due to a ‘breach of allegiance to the State of Israel.’” Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir on Monday said military lawyers were examining “possible legal measures concerning the film and those involved in it,” accusing them of “blood libels, deliberate distortions of reality and grave, false accusations against IDF soldiers and commanders.” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also publicly denounced the filmmakers and their documentary, which won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice International Film Festival. Member of Knesset and former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman called Abraham and Szor “haters of Israel,” while the former prime minister Naftali Bennett described the film, titled with an IDF acronym for “collateral damage,” as “a horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters.” “Israeli authorities must ensure the safety of Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and immediately reject any attempt to use citizenship rights as a weapon against journalists,” said CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah. “Threats from senior government officials can have a chilling effect on journalists and encourage members of the public to engage in intimidation and silencing against them. These threats cannot be dismissed as political rhetoric. They are a warning to journalists and sources about the potential consequences of reporting critically on powerful institutions—and a dangerous signal to other journalists considering whether to investigate or expose alleged wrongdoing.” Since October 2023, CPJ has documented widespread attacks and restrictions against journalists covering the Israel-Gaza war. Israeli and international journalists working in Israel and the occupied West Bank have faced threats and physical assaults, while Palestinian journalists and media workers in Gaza have been killed, arrested, and detained, and faced restrictions on their ability to report. In February 2024, Abraham received death threats after he and Palestinian co-director Basel Adra won awards at the Berlin International Film Festival for “No Other Land.” Abraham canceled his flight home after a right-wing Israeli mob threatened his family at their home, forcing them to flee overnight. In response to an email requesting comment, the Israeli military referred CPJ to the “political echelon.” The prime minister’s office and culture ministry did not respond by the time of publication. On the evening of September 10, unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle fired gunshots at the office of La Noticia Clave in the northern town of Lambayeque near the Pacific coast, according to the National Association of Journalists of Peru (ANP) and the Lima-based Institute for Press and Society (IPYS). The gunmen shot four times at the office while La Noticia Clave director Johnny Namuche and another journalist were inside the building, Namuche told CPJ in a voice message. He said the news outlet had not previously been threatened but said the attack came in the wake of a La Noticia Clave report about possible medical malpractice by a local hospital. “This attack highlights the dangerous environment that Peruvian local media outlets face when reporting on matters of public interest against all odds,” said Cristina Zahar, CPJ Latin America program coordinator, in São Paulo. “The Peruvian authorities must fight impunity by identifying and holding those responsible to account.” In a May 2026 special report , CPJ found that the targeting of reporters by criminal groups has contributed to a steady erosion of press freedom in Peru. CPJ’s email to the press department of the Attorney General’s office in Lima did not receive a reply. Conflict News 18 May 2026 M23 tax drive in DR Congo puts squeeze on aid groups Read more about... The M23 rebellion Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email GOMA, Democratic Republic of the Congo Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have embedded themselves into the local economy of eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, using revenue from taxes and minerals to pay fighters, maintain an administration, and consolidate territory. But the system faces constraints: The rebels and their backers are extracting revenue from an economy weakened by war, disrupted trade, and the collapse of formal banking, while lacking the financial infrastructure needed to revive it. “The M23 spoke of liberation, but economically the situation is even worse than before,” said a shop owner in Goma, the largest city in eastern DRC. “The airport is closed, there are no banks, businesses have shut, people have no money to buy... we are just surviving.” The M23 began its latest insurgency in 2021, seizing large tracts of territory before capturing the two main cities in the east – Goma and Bukavu – in early 2025. It now acts as a de facto governing power in an area where millions of people live. Taxation forms the backbone of its financing system, extending from local companies and markets to transporters, cross-border businesses, ordinary residents, and even humanitarian organisations . To cement its system and have greater autonomy in areas it controls, the rebels have also set up a parallel financial system, though these efforts have not yet proved especially successful. Minerals like gold and coltan constitute another important part of the M23’s war chest, with lucrative mining sites and transport corridors subject to taxation and resource extraction. Many of these minerals are smuggled across the border to the M23’s chief backer, Rwanda, which has thousands of soldiers on Congolese soil fighting alongside and commanding rebel operations. The flow of minerals and other goods through Rwanda and onto global markets has intensified scrutiny of international complicity in the violence, and the wider exploitation of Congolese resources – a pattern stretching from Belgian colonial rule to today’s extractive capitalism. “Criminal governance” Much of the conflict in eastern DRC traces back to the 1990s after the genocide of the Tutsi in Rwanda. When Hutu genocidaires fled into eastern DRC, Rwanda’s new government followed them, backing rebels who challenged and toppled Congolese administrations. The Tutsi-led M23 – the latest in a long line of Rwanda-backed insurgents – initially justified its rebellion by accusing the Congolese government of failing to implement a previous peace deal with the group, and by citing threats to local Tutsi communities. While denying direct support to the M23, Kigali justifies the group’s fight on the grounds that genocidaires remain active in eastern DRC. Critics, however, say it is using the threat as a pretext for territorial expansion and economic exploitation. As the insurgency has expanded, the M23 has developed national ambitions under a political wing, the Congo River Alliance (AFC in French). They have called for the removal of Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi and threatened to march on Kinshasa. The rebels have “methodically consolidated a de facto, deeply illegal, parallel administration”, said Zobel Behalal, an expert at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime and a former member of the UN experts panel on DRC. Behalal told The New Humanitarian that the “forms of criminal governance” created by the M23/AFC leave civilians with no choice but to finance the group, despite it being under UN and other international sanctions. Much of the financing takes the form of taxes. Every day in rebel areas, trucks carrying goods pay fees at checkpoints, as do motorbike taxis moving between towns. Businesses, from shops and warehouses to informal traders, are also taxed. Cross-border trade is another lucrative area for the group, with fees levied on fuel, agricultural goods, timber, charcoal, and manufactured products that pass through M23/AFC territory from and into Rwanda and Uganda. “Before the war, our products easily passed through national army checkpoints and reached our customers in different areas. Since then, we have encountered significant difficulties.” Though individually modest, these taxes provide the group with a steady and predictable income stream that helps maintain a quasi-state administration overseeing policing, justice, migration, customs, and other services. At the same time, if too burdensome, the taxes risk undermining businesses already struggling in a difficult economic environment, ultimately shrinking the group’s revenue base. A local businessman who opened a drinks factory four years ago said taxes paid to the M23/AFC contributed to the closure of his company. He also cited rising transport costs caused by the need to pass through multiple armed-group checkpoints. “Before the war, our products easily passed through national army checkpoints and reached our customers in different areas,” he said. “Since then, we have encountered significant difficulties.” Though some M23/AFC taxes already existed under the previous administration, there are additional levies that did not, as well as requirements for businesses to pay new registration fees, said Pascal Ndyanabo, an economist based in Goma. Businesses are also unable to negotiate manageable installments for paying taxes, he added: “The biggest difference is that, previously, it was possible to negotiate or stagger payments. Today, if you can’t pay, who will you complain to?” Tax squeeze Ordinary civilians also find themselves directly financing the group, through making payments for services such as water and electricity, and for requesting documents like land titles and vehicle records. Some of these services are run by public entities that have been administratively taken over by the M23/AFC, while others are run by private companies that pay a fee to the rebels. In some areas, residents also describe being required to contribute cash, labour, or goods. The rebels will often gather people and ask them to unload trucks, repair roads, build structures, or hand over part of their harvest to troops. At the same time, however, the M23/AFC cannot squeeze the population and local business to the point where deepening poverty and hunger further undermine its already limited legitimacy. Many people are struggling deeply with the economic situation: The airport in Goma is closed, complicating deliveries of aid and imported goods; and ongoing fighting is preventing people from cultivating land and getting produce to the markets. The closure of the formal banking system has added to the economic strain. Shortly after the M23/AFC took Goma, the government in Kinshasa ordered banks in rebel-held areas to shut. Trade was soon paralysed, wages were frozen, and many people were cut off from their savings and access to loans. Money changers said exchange rates and shortages of foreign currency have forced them to source cash in Rwanda. “Most of the transactions and trade now go through Rwanda. It is an expensive solution for both the population and the economic actors,” said Behalal, of the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime. To circumvent the banking shutdown, the movement has attempted to revive the Caisse Générale d'Épargne du Congo (CADECO), a public financial institution that was created in 1950 and offers a range of financial services. But while some CADECO branches have opened in Goma and Bukavu, they are disconnected from the national banking system and have no access to SWIFT, which is essential for international transfer

https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-.body: Home Middle East and North Africa Yemen Related stories Conflict Analysis 14 September 2026 How Rwanda-backed M23 rebels finance their war in DR Congo Conflict Opinion 11 September 2026 Visible crises, invisible people Conflict Analysis 9 September 2026 Finding a path to peace: Nigeria’s long, faltering history of dialogue with Boko Haram Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email TAIZ, Yemen Some 125,000 people have been forced from their homes across Yemen in the past two weeks as a major new escalation linked to both the US-Iran conflict and Yemen’s own nearly 12-year war deepens hardship for millions already struggling to survive. Hafedhaa Murshed had spent more than five years in a displacement site in western Taiz province before clashes broke out on 3 September near the site where she, her husband, and their seven children were staying. As the fighting drew nearer, the family grabbed their most valuable and lightest possessions. “We walked nearly three kilometres on foot,” Murshed told The New Humanitarian, speaking from the makeshift camp elsewhere in Taiz where they are now staying. “There were no vehicles to transport our belongings, so we arrived here with only a few kitchen utensils and a blanket.” Taiz has long been a flashpoint of Yemen’s war. Fighting, sieges, and restrictions on aid and trade access have been hallmarks of life in the southwestern province for years . Houthi rebels and a coalition of fighters allied with the internationally recognised government have been fighting since early 2015, and Taiz lies between territory currently controlled by the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government. A 2022 truce had ushered in a period of relative calm, but the Houthis (officially called Ansar Allah) launched an offensive on multiple fronts in early September, part of their bid to control the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait. Saudi Arabia has hit back with airstrikes and the United States has reportedly sent advisers to aid the kingdom’s military efforts, raising fears of a return to all-out war. Controlling the strait allows the Houthis – who have ties to Iran – to further block Saudi Arabia from exporting oil via the Red Sea (the kingdom has been using the strait to export oil since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz). It is also part of the longstanding stated goal of the Houthis to take the Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed fighters. While the reasons behind the new offensive are murky and complex, the impact on Yemen’s most vulnerable civilians – among them more than 5.2 million who were already displaced before this uptick in fighting – have been clear and direct. Like many others, Murshed was already dealing with extreme poverty before her latest displacement. But she had been staying with another displaced relative, who at least shared their mattresses and blankets. The UN reports that 125,000 people have been newly displaced in just two weeks and the numbers are rising quickly – including tens of thousands in Taiz alone . Entire communities are being forced from their homes, and some are now fleeing the country altogether, with the UN’s migration agency reporting that 2,000 people have reached Djibouti's northern shores . With the response to Yemen’s humanitarian crisis already chronically underfunded, and now compounded by the economic impacts of the US-Iran war, people like Murshed are finding themselves trapped in an endless cycle of displacement, with little to no assistance. “Our life wasn’t perfect, but at least we had a safe camp,” Murshed said of life at the previous site, which was already her family’s second displacement. “The fighting has forced us to flee again, and to begin the suffering of displacement and starting from scratch again.” Khalid Al-Banna/TNH When Hafedhaa Murshed fled the camp where she lived with her family for the past five years, she was only able to take a few cooking supplies and a blanket. Fuel prices and day wages Long before Murshed and her family were forced to leave their camp, Yemen’s economic crisis was already battering people like her far from the front lines. “Even before we fled last week, we lacked many of the basics because work opportunities were scarcer than before. Men would leave in the morning looking for work and return by midday empty-handed,” Murshed explained. The growing regional fallout from the Iran-US conflict triggered a sharp surge in fuel prices across government-controlled areas in Yemen. A 20-litre container of diesel has jumped from 25,000 YER ($17) in May – several months after the war began – to 45,000 YER ($30) today. A source at the Yemeni Petroleum Company in Aden told Reuters in May that the rise in fuel prices – even back then – was the result of a supply crisis and rising global fuel prices driven by the regional conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. That surge has had a cascading effect since, driving up the cost of goods and services that are dependent on fuel and transportation – including construction materials – hitting day labourers first. The only jobs that many displaced men like Murshed’s husband can get now are day-by-day jobs on construction sites or loading and unloading building supplies at local shops. “I don’t remember a time in my life when we ate only bread and tea for breakfast and dinner like we do now. We buy just enough food to stay alive because our income doesn't allow for more, and we can't afford the food we actually want.” Murad Thabet, a construction worker in his 50s who has worked in the industry across various parts of Yemen, described the current crisis as “the worst in his life”. “I have been working for around 40 years, but these days are the worst,” he told The New Humanitarian. “The price of building materials is rising dramatically, so many contractors and property owners have halted work until things stabilise.” Thabet, who is displaced from his village in the southwest of the province and rents a home in Taiz city for his wife and three children, said many day labourers are struggling to provide their families with basic necessities. “I don’t remember a time in my life when we ate only bread and tea for breakfast and dinner like we do now,” he added. “We buy just enough food to stay alive because our income doesn't allow for more, and we can't afford the food we actually want.” Thabet stressed that his main problem is the lack of job opportunities rather than the cost of food itself. This has long been the case in Yemen, where economic collapse as a result of their own 12-year war has been a major driver of hunger. US-funded food insecurity monitor FEWS NET has consistently said that displaced people and those without income are of greatest concern across a country where 15-16 million people are expected to need food aid through September – not taking into account this month’s developments. “If we have an income, we can buy food even if prices rise a bit,” said Thabet. “But when we have no work, as is the case now, we cannot afford food even if it is cheap.” Nasser al-Sakkaf/TNH In Taiz, construction remains one of the few jobs open to displaced people, 4 July 2026. Competition and sacrifice Thabet said he is among many men who wait at the same spot in Taiz every morning looking for work. Most leave disappointed. “When someone arrives looking for one labourer, around 10 people run after him and accept any wage because they desperately need work,” he said. Abdullah Mohammed, a displaced father of three in his late 30s, recently lost his job as a construction worker and guard at a building site in Taiz. https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/analy.body: Home Global Related stories Aid and Policy Cheat Sheet 11 September 2026 UK condemns “settler terrorists”, Sudan’s chemical weapons exposed, and Yemen’s war escalates Aid and Policy Interview 10 September 2026 “When do you put your foot down?” Why this de-mining group is rejecting US funding Aid and Policy Podcasts 10 September 2026 Rethinking Humanitarianism | Will aid-for-hire become the new normal? Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email GENEVA The Trump administration dismantled aid and attacked the global system as wasteful. Now a Trump pick looks set to lead one of the world’s biggest humanitarian agencies. US agriculture official Luke Lindberg will be named the new head of the World Food Programme, two aid officials familiar with the selection process told The New Humanitarian. Officially, the UN secretary-general and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s director-general choose the WFP leader, in consultation with WFP’s executive board. A special session of WFP’s board is scheduled for 18 September. A letter shared within humanitarian circles also confirms Lindberg as the pick. News of Lindberg’s pending appointment was first reported by Devex over the weekend. Is the World Food Programme getting Luke Lindberg, “America First” Trump appointee, or Luke Lindberg, rookie international civil servant and impartial humanitarian leader? It follows months-long delays in choosing a new executive director at WFP – and for some, worry over what putting a Trump-aligned pick at the heart of the emergency aid system will mean. WFP has been without an official executive director since Cindy McCain announced her departure earlier this year, citing health concerns. Lindberg’s selection would continue a long history of opaque UN appointments and American dominance at the helm of WFP. The executive director role has been held by an American since 1992, under the UN’s practice of backroom horse-trading key roles. It’s also another example of top leadership jobs going to the politically connected, whether at UN agencies or big NGOs . Lindberg is the son-in-law of US Senate majority leader John Thune , and currently undersecretary for trade and foreign agricultural affairs in the US Department of Agriculture. Lindberg appears to have no experience in emergency response, but he will join a UN agency that is often seen as the lynchpin of the international humanitarian system. His public record so far contrasts sharply with the neutrality and impartiality principles that the humanitarian sector often foregrounds. Lindberg has voiced support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (who has an active arrest warrant for war crimes accusations), and touted weapons exports amid the Israeli military’s onslaught on Gaza. Critics say the US is increasingly co-opting the humanitarian system along ideological lines – using funding and policy to align aid with geopolitical interests , and to sideline reproductive health and equity, for example. Lindberg will lead a key agency at a time of deep budget cuts, severe hunger, and spiralling emergencies – in some cases in crises provoked by US military actions and US government policies. Some 151.6 million people face crisis levels of hunger or worse, according to famine analysts . Crises are spiralling, deepened by conflict, climate change, and the flouting of international laws. At the same time, donor funding cuts have left the global emergency response system at a breaking point , triaging budgets to target only a fraction of the more than 239 million people said to need emergency aid. WFP’s projected funding this year sits at around $6.4 billion – less than half of what it was in 2022 , and its lowest in about a decade. The US funds about 30% of the agency’s budget. Here are four key questions: Who does Lindberg answer to? Is the World Food Programme getting Luke Lindberg, “America First” Trump appointee, or Luke Lindberg, rookie international civil servant and impartial humanitarian leader? The Trump administration has used foreign aid funding as a hammer: It steers its humanitarian and health money to align with geopolitical interests instead of needs; and sharpened its discriminatory global gag rule to sideline reproductive health and equity programmes funded by other donors. This has put an extra spotlight on the delayed search for a new WFP chief. Will they be beholden to Washington, or to the organisation’s humanitarian mandate? “We never really had to ask this question before for a UN appointee quite so explicitly,” said Sam Vigersky, a former US humanitarian adviser and now a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a New York-based think tank. “That to me in itself is a concerning development in our field.” Before the Trump administration backed Lindberg for the UN role, other rumoured candidates had pushed to make US support to WFP conditional on aligning with foreign policy interests, Vigersky said. Lindberg hasn’t outlined such plans, and should be judged based on what he does when he starts at WFP, he said. “Is Lindberg able to unlock sums of money from the Congress and the Trump administration that otherwise would be sidelined because there wasn’t an insider at the helm... or does this end up being an appointment to a multilateral agency that ends up running a political operation for the Trump administration to potentially be punitive towards NGOs they think are critical of the administration,” Vigersky said. “A lot of the aid coming out of [the] State Department has directly framed how they are making decisions. So I’m going to be looking for the firewall between the two.” Many of the issues at the heart of WFP’s work may contradict the current US administration’s interests – from climate change as a cause of crises, to famine declarations that are politically inconvenient for allies like Israel, to pushing back on aid cuts. Still a US government official for now, Lindberg’s recent public comments have defended the cuts as a sort of “level-setting”. ”This idea that we’re retreating is an unfair characterisation of the pause that was taken to re-evaluate and re-design some of the structures and the way in which we do business,” Lindberg said during a CFR briefing this month. A study in The Lancet estimated that donor cuts could lead to 9.4 million deaths by 2030. In his short time in the agriculture department, Lindberg has been open about using US aid for US interests. The USDA-managed Food for Peace programme, which sends US commodities as food assistance, now targets only a handful of countries , after a restructuring overseen by Lindberg. It notably leaves out several countries facing severe levels of hunger – such as Mali, Somalia, Sudan, or Yemen – while including some that are not. These choices balanced hunger needs, the availability of distribution partners, and “the geopolitical interests of the United States”, Lindberg said . How do other humanitarian agencies see Lindberg? Lindberg is mostly unknown in humanitarian circles, but his social media feed has done most of the talking so far. His personal accounts have been peppered with pro-Israel posts, pics of Lindberg grinning and gripping a rifle to be exported to the Israeli military, and plenty of cowboy hats. A newer Twitter account created for his WFP bid presents a milder image, tinted with shades of UN blue, frequent retweets of WFP posts, and inoffensive statements about resilience and ending hunger. Lindberg is “obviously MAGA” and the gun pics are concerning, but he appears to be less risky than other names floated for key positions, one aid official told The New Humanitarian. “Basically, I think he’s someone we can work with,” said the official, who compared Lindberg’s potential to that of David Beasley, the former South Carolina governor appointed as WFP executive director during Trump’s first term. https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news/.body: Home Americas This article is also available in French Arabic Share & more Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email NAIROBI NAIROBI, 2 November 2011 (IRIN) - More than 18 months since the earthquake struck Haiti in January 2010, women and girls living in makeshift camps remain vulnerable to sexual violence. IRIN's latest film follows a survivor of rape, Shirley Christoff, as she attempts to rebuild her life in a rundown informal settlement in Port-au-Prince. Christoff, together with thousands of other women, lives in constant fear for her safety. According to human rights organizations, continued lack of security is one of the main factors contributing to high levels of rape in and around the internal displacement camps. More than 250 cases of rape were reported in several camps in the first 150 days after the earthquake, according to Amnesty International. Sexual violence and other forms of gender-based violence were widespread in Haiti even before the earthquake. In the 1990s, Human Rights Watch (HRW) documented the use of rape as a form of oppression during the regime of Raoul Cédras. From 2004 to 2006, the UN Security Council estimated that 35,000 women and girls were subjected to rape and sexual violence. "After you have been raped, you have nowhere to go, you have to return to the camp and face the person who raped you," says Christoff. As police stations and courts were reduced to rubble during the earthquake, the few protection mechanisms that did exist were destroyed. According to Amnesty and HRW, the post-earthquake humanitarian and government response to gender-based violence has been wholly inadequate. While effort was being invested to ensure basic needs were met, little to no attention has been paid to the rights of women and girls to be protected from sexual violence. Survivors of sexual violence have taken matters into their own hands, with two grassroots organizations providing support to thousands of women. The first emergency response system dedicated to sexual violence was set up in October and a call centre has already recorded 400 cases of rape. This film is the 10th in a series of films about displacement, Forced to Flee. Others in the series include Bolivia’s Changing Climate , Israel’s African Migrants and Haiti’s Homeless Hotel . Home Southern Africa Eswatini Related stories Human Rights News 4 December 2024 “Independence day”: Diego Garcia asylum seekers celebrate arrival in UK Human Rights News 15 January 2024 Asylum seekers sent by UK to Rwanda report sexual abuse and harassment Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email Warning: This story contains descriptions of self-harm and suicide. BANGKOK A Sri Lankan Tamil asylum seeker detained by the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) administration for nearly five years died by apparent suicide on 13 September in Mbabane, Eswatini’s largest city, according to local news reports and relatives of the deceased. His death comes two years after the BIOT administration granted him international protection, preventing his forcible return to Sri Lanka, during which time he lived in a legal limbo in multiple countries. Kishanth Peramaiya, 36, was one of 89 Tamil asylum seekers who had fled Sri Lanka and India before being rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when their fishing vessel faltered near the British-held island of Diego Garcia, which lies within BIOT. Hundreds of additional arrivals followed on later vessels, most of whom agreed to return to Sri Lanka or left by boat to Mauritius or the French island of Réunion. Around 60 remained in BIOT custody, living in a fenced tent camp in Diego Garcia’s tightly controlled UK-US military facility. They faced rat infestations, deteriorating psychological and medical conditions, and the threat of being prosecuted or shot if they violated strict movement restrictions. Most were approved to enter the UK in November 2024. The following month, the BIOT Supreme Court ruled their detention on the island had been unlawful. But Kishanth was one of three members of the group denied entry to the UK because they had been convicted of crimes or were under criminal investigation during their detention. Another is serving the remainder of a three-year prison sentence in Montserrat for sexual offences against a child; and the third appeared to be serving a sentence on Diego Garcia for an undisclosed crime as of April 2026. Kishanth’s case, according to analysis by the London-based GSC Solicitors, “underscores the complexities of balancing humanitarian considerations with public safety concerns”. His transfer to Eswatini and subsequent death raise further questions about how the UK government decided to address these complexities, particularly since his suicidality was known to UK authorities for years. Local media in Eswatini have reported that his transfer to the country was permanent. If confirmed, it would appear to be the first publicly documented instance of an asylum seeker being granted international protection by a British authority before being permanently resettled in a different country. The closest precedent was a 2022 plan to send asylum seekers from the UK to Rwanda for processing and potential resettlement. This faced legal challenges and was scrapped in 2024 before transfers began. Three asylum seekers sent from Diego Garcia to Rwanda in 2023 for medical treatment said they were harassed or threatened there, including by a hospital worker. The New Humanitarian spoke by phone on 15 September to Kishanth’s relatives in India, which hosts a large, effectively stateless Sri Lankan Tamil population. His mother said he was transferred from Diego Garcia to the Maldives six months ago because of the US-Iran war. A month later, she said, he was brought to Eswatini, where he received two successive three-month visas, the second of which was due to expire on 20 September. Swaziland News reported in July that an agreement between the UK and Eswatini governments allowed Kishanth to stay in the country permanently. “At the end of the period of up to three years, the UK will no longer cover any costs of the continued presence of the Relocated Migrant in Eswatini. The Relocated Migrant is expected to be self-sustaining as a member of Eswatini society,” reads an excerpt of the agreement, according to the local outlet. An Eswatini lawmaker criticised the country’s prime minister for turning the country into a “dumping ground” by admitting a “delinquent” from Sri Lanka. On 15 September, the Times of Eswatini reported that a Sri Lankan national “was found hanging from the rafters at a guest house” the previous weekend, prompting a police investigation. The New Humanitarian has approached the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and the BIOT administration for clarification on Kishanth’s status in Eswatini and the circumstances surrounding his death. Toufique Hossain of Duncan Lewis Solicitors, which represented Kishanth in legal challenges to the UK and BIOT governments, said he was not authorised to comment. Kishanth had been “ tortured, sexually assaulted and abused ” by Sri Lankan military personnel before fleeing to India in 2007. He was one of eight members of the Diego Garcia group to be granted international protection on the basis of individual assessments, some on similar grounds. But he was barred from entering the UK with the rest of the group because of a series of criminal convictions: sexually assaulting another asylum seeker four times, assaulting and harming a security officer who tried to intervene in his suicide attempt, and arson “ in connection with an attempted suicide by self-immolation ”. “Whilst we understand the need to separate him from the community, his right to privacy and to be accommodated in a humane and dignified manner must be upheld.” In response to his behaviour and unravelling mental state, BIOT authorities kept him separate from the rest of the asylum seeker group. He was confined for around eight months in a laundry room with only supervised access to other areas of the compound and two weeks alone in a police cell with no natural light. Following a late 2023 monitoring visit, UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, said it was “ deeply concerned ” by the conditions of his detention, citing his sleeping area’s exposure to noise, shower leaks, and toilet smells. “Whilst we understand the need to separate him from the community, his right to privacy and to be accommodated in a humane and dignified manner must be upheld,” the monitoring team said in a 2024 report. Throughout his detention, he attempted suicide numerous times, sometimes in quick succession, prompting medical evacuation to Bahrain in 2024, according to court records. The New Humanitarian spoke briefly with Kishanth following his return to Diego Garcia from medical treatment in Rwanda in 2023. In broken English, he described receiving “not correct treatment”, “no sleeping”, and being confined to a “military area”. Another asylum seeker recalled witnessing him “walking alone”, “seeing dreams”, “screaming at night”, and threatening to harm himself with a shard of a broken mirror. A psychiatrist quoted in 2024 court proceedings said “it is very difficult for him to be so isolated for an indefinite period”, and ending his isolation “would hugely improve his mental health”. In 2025, a UK court dismissed Kishanth’s legal challenge to being barred from the country, allowing the government to base its decision on public safety concerns. With return to Sri Lanka ruled out and the UK refusing him admission, his only remaining solution was relocation to a third country. His mother told The New Humanitarian he sounded depressed when they spoke on 13 September, the same day his body was found. She had asked him to come back to India. Seemingly unaware or disbelieving his stay in Eswatini was permanent, he told his mother he was planning on waiting there for a few days before being sent to a third country.
